#64238. Tech Report: 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad

Tech Report: 45 AD-Approved International Interior Photographers to Know for Your Next Project Abroad

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2471 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, they jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes.
  • In a recent development, born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography.
  • A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, they jet around the globe, camera in hand, capturing expansive views from clifftop villas and intimate reading nooks in private homes. The international interior photographers on these pages don’t just record living spaces; they tell stories and create moods, turning their eyes to details such as the light streaming through a red curtain or a marble statue waiting to welcome guests into a villa’s entryway. Each image is infused with a sense of place and the spirit of the people who pass through it. Read on to discover top talents working in Europe, Asia, Oceania, North Africa, South America, and Canada.

Interior by Marie-Anne Derville.

In a recent development, born in South Korea, raised in Chicago, and currently living and working in Paris, Matthew Avignone brings a truly international perspective to his photography. His images often center around the collected objects that make a space personal and give it life.

A bathroom in Cap Martin along the French Riviera, designed by Studio Humbert & Poyet.

With Harry Nuriev, Festen, and Bernard Dubois among his collaborators, Ludovic Balay is no stranger to interiors with a point of view. The Paris photographer’s roster also includes Halleroed, adding another distinctive design voice to the picture.

The drawing room of a Notting Hill home designed by Olivia Williams.

Henry Bourne’s photographs open a window into creative people’s private worlds. The UK photographer’s interiors and portrait work includes subjects such as John Pawson, Faye Toogood, Luca Guadagnino, and Rose Uniacke.

A London townhouse designed by AD100 designer Leonora Hamill.

Recent findings suggest that helen Cathcart brings a painterly, atmospheric quality to her work, which has resonated with some of the world’s hottest brands, designers, and publications. Cathcart’s photos of interiors, in particular, proffer serenity and calm through their tonality.

It has been revealed that the Row, Lemaire, and a host of AD interiors: François Coquerel’s portfolio is in very good company. The Paris photographer moves between fashion and design, with Massimo Adario and Oitoemponto among his architectural collaborators.

Designer Luca Cipelletti delivers architectural precision and material opulence to an art collector’s Porta Nuova apartment.

According to recent reports, partners in life and work, Michael Depasquale and Martina Maffini count industry names like Dimore Studio, Nilufar Gallery, and JW Anderson among their clients. The duo splits their time between Paris and Milan and injects dynamism into each shoot that becomes evident in the final, glossy-ready results.

A villa in New Zealand by Patterson Associates.

According to recent reports, simon Devitt doesn’t stop at photographing architecture: fine art photo books, exhibitions, and workshops also fill his calendar. Based in Wellington, he has worked with Fearon Hay, Shigeru Ban, and Olson Kundig, documenting buildings across New Zealand and beyond.

Joseph Dirand’s Paris apartment.

Joseph Dirand designs rooms; his brother Adrien photographs them, including the architect’s Paris apartment for AD. Also based in Paris, Adrien contributed photography to the book Joseph Dirand Interior. A creative family, to say the least.

Inside the Paris headquarters of ACNE studios.

Industry observers note that having started his career in fashion, Dol Maillot is as beloved for his street style shots and travel photography as he is for his interiors. Born in the South of France, the globetrotting artist now lives in Paris.

A Kelly Behun apartment at London’s Whiteley hotel is just one reason to linger over Veerle Evens’s portfolio. The London photographer moves between interiors, food, and travel, with HBA Residential, Owl Design, and Christian Bense among her collaborators.

A color-drenched home in the Canary Islands.

According to recent reports, some interiors tell you as much about their owners as a portrait might. Miguel Flores-Vianna seeks out those personal worlds, bringing his curiosity not just to interiors but also to his books, including Haute Bohemians and Haute Bohemians Greece. Armchair travelers, settle in.

Recent findings suggest that join the AD PRO Directory, AD’s professional network that gives you access to exclusive events and exposure to the future clients. Learn more.

Inside the Paris apartment of Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, as seen in AD France.

Among international interior photographers, Jérôme Galland ups the ante with his photos through a combination of striking contrasts, dramatic angles, and an appreciation of scale. French châteaus, Italian palazzos, and Greek villas all appear at their most grand through his lens.

Sources indicate that venetian interiors and Moroccan retreats make tempting subjects: Kasia Gatkowska’s portfolio travels well. The Amsterdam-based photographer has worked with Vincenzo De Cotiis, Vincent Van Duysen, Axel Vervoordt, and Massimo Adario, among others.

The home of the ABC Concept founders in Karuizawa, Japan.

In a recent development, kenzo Takada’s Paris home is just one stop in Mitchell Geng’s portfolio. The Tokyo photographer also captured a colorful Hong Kong residence for Vogue Hong Kong and includes architecture, interiors, and hospitality in his photographic itinerary.

A Paris apartment by Pierre Yovanovitch.

Film buffs may recognize Luca Guadagnino, the Italian director, producer, and screenwriter behind films such as Call Me By Your Name; design lovers will know his interiors too. Milan photographer Giulio Ghirardi has worked with the multihyphenate, shooting his interior design projects, and has also turned his lens to the work of Pierre Yovanovitch, Kelly Wearstler, Rodolphe Parente, and Augusta Hoffman.

A kitchen by AKB Design in Salaberry-de-Valleyfield, Quebec.

Industry observers note that whether she is shooting portraits, food, travel, or interiors, Sylvie Li’s commercial and editorial images build a narrative. Just look at how she commemorates the marriage of old and new in this renovated Montreal apartment which appeared in AD.

The reception room of the barn on designer Jean-Louis Denoit’s watercress farm in France.

If Laura Gonzalez, Hugo Toro, and Pierre Yovanovitch feature on your list of design heroes, Stephan Julliard’s portfolio warrants a visit. The Paris photographer has worked with all three, as well as Jean-Louis Deniot, Kelly Wearstler, and Greg Natale.

Designer Meg Sharpe turns a traditional warren of rooms into an airy idyll where livability and flair are winsome bedfellows.

Having shot for Dimorestudio, MacGuffin, Icon, and—hello, AD—Kyle Knodell has a knack for producing interior photos filled with life. At AD, we’ve tapped him to photograph Samantha Angelo and Peter Ostrega in their LES home.

The Paris apartment belonging to Gregoire Marot and Thomas Dupré de St Maur, designed with help of their friend the designer Eric Allart.

Spain and Uruguay make appealing bookends for Ricardo Labougle’s practice. In between, his lens takes in interiors, gardens, and portraits, with the work of Jacques Grange, Vincent Van Duysen, Studio KO, and Michael S. Smith among its subjects.

A Stockholm apartment designed by Studio Escapist.

From OMA’s architecture to Max Lamb’s furniture, Erik Lefvander moves easily between subjects, thrilling design enthusiasts. The Stockholm photographer’s collaborators also include Halleroed, Sabine Marcelis, and Sophie Dries.

Tour a London pied-à-terre by Studio Ashby that’s a dazzling foray into maximalism.

“Uplifting” is the best way to describe Kensington Leverne’s photography, thanks to the softness and warmth that her images exude. Whether the interiors she shoots are palatial or cozy, Leverne is able to evoke a sense of intimacy within each space.

A bedroom in Stockholm’s Ett Hem boutique hotel.

According to recent reports, magnus Mårding takes a natural approach, whether the subject is a person, a car, or an interior. Based in Stockholm, he has worked with Ilse Crawford, Michael S. Smith, and Olson Kundig. Different subjects, one curious eye.

A villa near Venice by MIDE Architetti.

According to recent reports, giulia Maretti can help set the scene as well as photograph it. The Bologna- and Berlin-based MAGI Studio cofounder combines photography, styling, and art direction, and has worked with the likes of MIDE Architetti and Studio Bosko.

A New York townhouse designed by Elizabeth Roberts Architects, Grace Fuller Marroquin, and Leonora Hamill.

Recent findings suggest that mexico City provides a fitting home base for Fernando Marroquin’s design-minded lens. His subject matter ranges from interiors to hospitality to retail, and he has worked with Héctor Esrawe, Manuel Cervantes, Ezequiel Farca, and Luis Laplace.

Gabriel Chipperfield and Laura de Gunzburg transformed their 19th-century London flat, blending contemporary softness with crisp minimalism.

Multiple shoots for AD and Vogue that show the English country manors and London town houses of the UK’s top celebrities and creatives fill Kate Martin’s portfolio. She adapts her eye for fashion editorial to interiors and portraits with ease.

Nicolas Matheus’s photos have graced the covers of countless international design magazines, depicting chic French apartments, sunny Spanish casas, coastal Cape Town villas, and more. His work in and around the Mediterranean is particularly gorgeous.

Still-life arrangements of smaller objects within larger spaces populate Alice Mesguich’s Instagram feed, showcasing her penchant for capturing styled vignettes as well as corners and niches she finds interesting.

A kitchen designed by Ashley Montgomery.

In a recent development, fans of Ashley Montgomery, Sam Sacks, and Ali Budd may already have Lauren Miller’s images on their inspiration boards. The Toronto photographer captures interiors and still lifes, with work appearing in AD and House & Garden.

Balmore House in North London, designed by Studio 163.

Architecture buffs will find familiar names in Peter Molloy’s orbit: O’Donnell + Tuomey, Grafton Architects, and Carmody Groarke, for starters. The London photographer has also worked with McLaren.Excell, keeping the built environment firmly in the frame.

In AD100 designer Vincenzo De Cotiis’s 15th-century Italian palazzo, a breccia baixa marble was chosen for its resemblance to the palazzo’s original ceiling, shown in this bath along with a circa 1895 Carlo Bugatti chair.

Sources indicate that textured surfaces—plasterwork, fabric, timber, you name it—are the first thing noticed in any interior shot by Martin Morrell, making him a favorite of designers like Vincenzo de Cotiis and Studio Peregalli. His full list of both editorial and advertising clients reads as a who’s who of brand and media.

According to recent reports, A dining area in the famed Casa de Canoas, a Brazilian modernist landmark designed by Oscar Niemeyer. Parente shot a campaign for Zara Home here.

According to recent reports, fran Parente travels his São Paulo–Newly introduced York circuit with some excellent design firm. Studio Arthur Casas, Studio MK27, Studio Mellone, and Isay Weinfeld figure among his collaborators, while hospitality, travel, and food broaden his view beyond architecture.

The pool area at the Desert Rock Resort in Saudi Arabia.

BIG. Kengo Kuma. Heatherwick Studio. Ema Peter’s collaborator list could double as an architecture lover’s hot list. Working between Vancouver and Los Angeles, she doesn’t just specialize in architecture; she also photographs residential interiors, including projects involving Studio Paolo Ferrari.

Proctor photographed the Brown Drawing Room at Blickling Hall in Norfolk as the house was being ‘put to sleep,’ a custom that involves draping the furniture when the visitor season ends, to allow the collections in the house to have some respite from the elements.

His intimate images of artists’ spaces and decorative arts workshops suggest Oskar Proctor enjoys looking behind the scenes. Working across London, Newly introduced York, and Los Angeles, he has shot the work of Soane Britain, Vanderhurd, and Jermaine Gallacher, among other design-world names.

A penthouse at One Park Drive, the Herzon & de Meuron building at London’s Canary Wharf.

Industry observers note that from the Aman New York to the Janu Tokyo, Robert Rieger’s portfolio makes a compelling case for checking in. The Berlin photographer also counts David Thulstrup, Vincent Van Duysen, and Herzog & de Meuron among his collaborators.

Designer Jacques Garcia’s 17th-century apartment in Paris.

Matthieu Salvaing’s book, Interior Voyages, lives up to its name, taking readers through homes as individual as their inhabitants. The Paris photographer’s travels encompass tropical retreats and historic residences, inviting readers to consider how different home can look around the world.

The bedroom of a Upcoming York townhouse designed by Greg Natale.

According to recent reports, if your design tastes travel from Flack Studio to Kelly Wearstler, Anson Smart’s portfolio connects the dots. The Sydney photographer also captures interiors by Arent & Pyke and Greg Natale, alongside hospitality and lifestyle assignments.

An apartment in Naples, Italy, designed by FADD Architects.

Architecture training gave Valentina Sommariva an insider’s introduction to the spaces she photographs. Objects get their moment, too, in the work of this Milan talent who also creates fine art projects that combine photography and video. Patricia Urquiola, Studiopepe, and Elisa Ossino Studio are among her collaborators.

The guest bedroom in Tarek Shamma’s London apartment.

Interiors by Child Studio and Holloway-Li make for quite the photographic playground. Working between London and New York, Felix Speller has photographed both, with Studio Hagen Hall and Lina Ghotmeh also among his other design subjects.

A London apartment designed by Douglas Mackie.

Sources indicate that if your design references lean British, put Astrid Templier on your radar. The London photographer’s collaborators include Guy Goodfellow, Douglas Mackie, Elicyon, and Rosanna Bossom—a roster that should resonate with fans of the English interior.

A private holiday home in Tuscany, Italy, designed by Vincenzo De Cotiis.

Industry observers note that A room can tell a story, and documentary photographer Ambroise Tézenas has an ear for the details. Based in Paris, he has photographed interiors by Luis Laplace, Jacques Garcia, and Vincenzo De Cotiis, including commissions for AD France.

The kitchen in Nate Berkus and Jeremiah Brent’s home in Portugal.

Recent findings suggest that trevor Tondro’s command of color and mood brings a lively quality to his interiors photography. With early experience assisting both Philip-Lorca diCorcia and Martyn Thompson, he maximizes both artificial and natural light, always finding more than one way into a room.

Historic Castle Howard in North Yorkshire, London.

According to recent reports, if you find Simon Upton’s list of subjects resembles your decorating bookshelf, that’s understandable. Rose Uniacke, Rita Konig, Michael S. Smith, and Stephen Sills are among the talents whose work the UK-based photographer has captured across continents.

Recent findings suggest that devotees of Belgian design, take note. Antwerp-based Frederik Vercruysse has worked with Axel Vervoordt, Vincent Van Duysen, and Muller Van Severen—a particularly appealing trio for anyone whose saved images run from contemplative interiors to playful furniture.

This home in the Swiss Alps by activist Nachson Mimran and AD100 talent Francis Kéré graced the cover of AD’s January 2025 glitch.

A farmhouse-inspired Manhattan apartment or a chalet in Megève? Cassie Floto Warner has photographed both for AD, including Amanda Seyfried’s Upcoming York apartment and a retreat by Elliott Barnes. The Paris-based photographer’s portfolio makes staying in sound particularly appealing.

The living room of a Venetian palazzo by architect Luca Bombassei.

Having tried his hand at film and painting, Watson settled on photography as his metier in the 1990s, and has had his work appear in magazines, books, ad campaigns, museums, and galleries in the United States and Europe. Although he works all over the globe, Watson now lives in Dublin, where he was born.

Latest Update: Toyota and Subaru hit the ‘sweet spot’ with affordable electric SUVs

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Toyota and Subaru’s latest electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.
  • The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.
  • Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Toyota and Subaru’s latest electric SUVs are catching on with buyers, offering various options and prices ranging from about $35,000 to $45,000, or the “sweet spot” of the US market.

The US electric vehicle market rebounded in the third quarter with 262,649 EVs sold, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates, up 6.1% from Q2 and the strongest performance of the year.

Although nearly every automaker has sold fewer EVs so far this year than in the same period in 2025, as buyers rushed to claim the $7,500 tax credit before it expired, a handful of brands are seeing considerably higher demand.

Outside of Rivian, Toyota and Subaru are the only brands that have higher year-over-year EV sales in the US through the third quarter.

Combined, Toyota and Subaru have sold nearly 50,000 EVs through the first nine months of 2026, more than double compared to the same period last year.

In a recent development, toyota alone has sold nearly 35,000 electric vehicles, up 183.4% YOY, while Subaru sold 14,630, up 46.7%. And that’s not even including the additional 12,676 sold under the Lexus brand, up 137.4% YOY.

While the two Japanese automakers were infamously slow to transition to battery electric vehicles, the timing worked in their favor.

It has been revealed that after launching the heavily updated bZ in late 2025, previously called the bZ4X, Toyota’s electric SUV suddenly became one of America’s most popular EVs. Through Q3, it was the fourth best-selling EV in the US, trailing only the Hyundai IONIQ 5, Tesla Model 3, and Tesla Model Y.

In a recent development, starting at $35,000, the Toyota bZ is one of the most affordable EVs in the US. It also offers up to 314 miles of range in the FWD Plus trim, which starts at $37,980.

Toyota and Subaru now each sell three electric SUVs, which share the same platform and technology.

With prices ranging from roughly $35,000 to about $45,000, Stephanie Valdez Streaty, director of industry insights at Cox Automotive, stated (via Bloomberg) Toyota and Subaru’s fresh EVs are affordable and hit the “sweet spot” of the US car market.

Toyota also sells the smaller, sporty C-HR, starting at $37,080, and the larger, more rugged bZ Woodland, which starts at $45,380.

Subaru, on the other hand, sells the updated Solterra ($38,495, plus the smaller Uncharted ($34,995) and midsize Trailseeker ($39,995).

Karla Fisher, a Marine and retired engineer, told Bloomberg that the Subaru Trailseeker was her “most favorite car of all time.”.

Industry observers note that while she considered buying an EV before the $7,500 federal credit expired last September, none met her requirements at the time. Fisher wanted at least 7″ of ground clearance, 250 miles or more range, and a price that was similar, or even less than a comparible gas-powered vehicle.

The Subaru Trailseeker offers all of that and starts at under $40,000. Toyota and Subaru’s electric SUVs all start at about $45,000 or less, which is even less than the average latest vehicle.

According to the latest Kelley Blue Book figures, the average price for a fresh vehicle in the US reached a record $51,109 in October, up 2.1% YOY.

Great as these may be, there is little inventory to be found.

There are less than 500 Uncharted available Nationwide.

You can't sell what you don't have. Yes, they can be ordered for sure, but how many missed sales does that model create?

Subaru spokesperson Dominick Infante said the affordable EV prices are mainly thanks to its partnership with Toyota. “We do believe there’s an EV future,” Infante added.

Next year, both brands will add a three-row electric SUV with the Toyota Highlander EV and Subaru Getaway.

Recent findings suggest that thinking about making the switch to an EV? With the 2027 models at dealerships, now could be a good time to find a deal on current 2026 models. You can use the links below to see what’s available at Toyota and Subaru dealerships near you.

Hyundai is shaking up its 2027 electric vehicle lineup: Here’s what’s changing

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (695 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the fresh IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.
  • Hyundai confirmed its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the latest IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.
  • While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hyundai’s US electric vehicle lineup will look a bit different in 2027, including the fresh IONIQ 6 N, a new range-topping IONIQ 9 trim, and a handful of minor updates to the IONIQ 5.

Hyundai confirmed its 2027 model-year changes on Wednesday, including the latest IONIQ 6 N and a few slight changes to the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9.

While Hyundai discontinued the standard IONIQ 6, it added the high-performance IONIQ 6 N for the 2027 lineup.

The IONIQ 6 N is Hyundai’s second performance EV, following the IONIQ 5 N. Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the electric sports car delivers a combined 641 hp and 568 lb-ft of torque.

Hyundai said the IONIQ 6 N can sprint from 0 to 60 mph in 3.2 seconds, beating the IONIQ 5 N at 3.25 seconds.

Like the IONIQ 5 N, it also includes fun added features, like N e-Shift and an N Active Sound+ system that simulates the sounds and sensations of a traditional gas-powered sports car with an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission.

It uses an 84 kWh battery that provides up to 245 miles of pure electric driving range. Thanks to its 800V ultra-fast charging architecture, the IONIQ 6 N can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes using a 350 kW DC fast charger.

Like Hyundai’s other electric vehicles, it comes standard with a native NACS charging port and a CCS adapter.

The 2027 IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 are mostly carryover models with a few minor changes, while the IONIQ 5 N remains the same as the 2026 model year.

Changes to the IONIQ 5 for the 2027 model year include roof rails, which are now available on the SEL trim and above; previously, they were only available on the XRT and Limited trims.

Hyundai HomeLink will be available exclusively on the Limited trim, rather than SEL and above, in the current 2026 model year, while the Cargo Cover will be offered as an Accessory only.

Regarding color options, the Gravity Gold Matte and Sage Silver Matte will no longer be available for the 2027 IONIQ 5.

The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 5 starts at $35,250, making it one of the most affordable EVs in the US.

That’s for the standard-range IONIQ 5 SE with an EPA-estimated range of up to 245 miles. The extended-range SE RWD model is $2,500 more, starting at $37,750, and offers up to 318 miles of range.

According to recent reports, hyundai’s three-row SUV also received a handful of updates. The 2027 Hyundai IONIQ 9 will be available with a fresh Calligraphy Black Ink trim, while the Calligraphy Design will no longer be offered.

The 2027 IONIQ 9 Calligraphy and Calligraphy Black Ink trims gain a Virtual Gear Shift and heated third-row seats. All variants also gain a Tailgate Emergency Lamp.

Recent findings suggest that on the one hand... the Ioniq5 is due for an upgrade. On the other... I still absolutely love the way it looks, and notice just about every one I pass on the road.

Hyundai has yet to announce prices for the 2027 model. The base 2026 IONIQ 9 S starts at $58,995 and offers an EPA-estimated driving range of up to 335 miles.

The previous top-spec Performance Calligraphy Design AWD started at $76,490, so you can expect the latest Calligraphy Black Ink to be around the same, if not even more.

It has been revealed that with the 2027 models on the way, you may be able to score some deals on Hyundai’s current EV lineup. Want to see what’s available near you? You can use the links below to find available Hyundai IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9 models near you, along with any current offers.

#64231. Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1052 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla confirms rare new delivery of 50 Semi electric trucks in Chicago

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1052 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.
  • Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its upcoming Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.
  • The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, reveals four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tesla has confirmed a new batch of Tesla Semi deliveries, with its official Semi account saying today that “Chicago’s first 50 Semis” are on their way to the city.

It’s a rare data point. Tesla doesn’t disclose Semi deliveries, and it claims its upcoming Nevada factory can build 50,000 of them a year.

The post, published on the @tesla_semi account on X at noon ET today, reveals four Semis lined up at sunset under the caption “Hello Windy City.” Tesla didn’t name the customer.

Hello Windy CityChicago’s first 50 Semis en route for delivery pic.twitter.com/75kig8yWsb.

But the only 50-truck Semi order tied to Chicago belongs to HMD Trucking. The family-owned carrier was founded in Chicago in 1998, runs more than 650 trucks (almost all diesel), and ordered 50 Semis right after Tesla’s production event in September.

Sources indicate that HMD took its first truck on November 2 and notes it’s the first Tesla Semi registered in Illinois. COO Michael Mahler said Tesla “has been transparent with us regarding the capabilities of Semi every step of the way.”.

Sources indicate that the organization ran a Semi for more than 4,000 miles over the summer and averaged 1.74 kWh per mile, right in line with Tesla’s 1.7 kWh/mile claim. The first trucks will mostly handle local runs around Chicago, and HMD is installing its own chargers there since Tesla’s Megacharger network is still concentrated along the I-5 and I-10 corridors in the West.

According to recent reports, owner Henry Malukas told MotorTrend the deal is worth about $15 million. That’s roughly $300,000 per truck, in line with the ~$290,000 Long Range pricing we reported when the first truck came off the high-volume line and a long way from the $180,000 Tesla advertised in 2017.

Here’s the problem: it’s nearly impossible to tell how many Semis Tesla is actually building.

Industry observers note that tesla launched volume production at its Sparks, Nevada factory on September 24, after pushing the ramp out of 2025. It indicates the 1.8 million sq ft plant is built for 50,000 trucks a year. But it never gave a ramp schedule, and its quarterly production and delivery reports only count “passenger vehicles sold to customers.” The Semi isn’t in there.

Recent findings suggest that so we’re left with proxies. Tesla indicates its Semi fleet has over 98% uptime, without saying how big that fleet is. Before this year, the largest Semi fleet was PepsiCo’s, at 86 trucks in 2024. California’s truck voucher program received 965 Semi applications between January 2025 and February 2026, which points to real demand but says nothing about output.

It has been revealed that the order book is the other clue. Einride ordered 500 Semis in August, WattEV has 370 on order, IMC Logistics wants 50 for California, and the ZET SCALE alliance picked Tesla as main supplier for 2,500 trucks. And now HMD’s 50 are rolling into Chicago, one of the first Semi fleets that will have to deal with a Midwest winter. Wisconsin’s Paper Transport has also been piloting a Semi in the Chicago market since the summer.

None of that adds up to a production rate, but it does look like Tesla is slowly ramping up deliveries.

Tesla keeps the Semi numbers vague on purpose. It’s happy to talk about a 50,000-truck-a-year factory, and it posts hero shots when a batch ships, but it won’t give the one number that reveals whether the factory is anywhere close to that.

I think the semi is going to be a major seller but its going to take some time to produce enough of them and for companies to gather enough data. Once the investment is justified, there will be customers and repeat customers. After that, it will only be a matter of time before other electric semi truck manufacturers start popping up with offerings and thats a good thing for everyone.

The 50,000 figure is what makes the Semi look like a real business to investors instead of a niche program that took nine years to get going. Tesla has a long history of quoting capacity long before it reaches it, so we shouldn’t treat “built for 50,000” as anything more than a ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that our read: Tesla is still far from that 50,000 rate. Fifty trucks for one customer is 0.1% of a year at full capacity, and if Tesla were shipping in large volumes, a single 50-unit batch wouldn’t get its own post. But the ramp has clearly started, the order book is real, and it’s plausible Tesla gets into the thousands by the end of the year.

Good for HMD, too. A 650-truck diesel fleet in a cold market is exactly the kind of customer the Semi has to win. Malukas admitted “we don’t have real numbers yet” on savings, and HMD’s own blog is fairly sober about cost and winter range. Local routes, depot charging and a Chicago winter is the right way to find out. It all sounds plausible for the Tesla Semi.

#64228. Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1118 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tesla extends Cybertruck production to late summer 2027 amid fan backlash

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first confirmed it was killing it.
  • The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a firm that sells cars to people.
  • It has been revealed that on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk now says Tesla will keep building the Cybertruck “through the end of summer 2027” to “work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog.” That buys the electric pickup roughly two to three more months, five days after Tesla first confirmed it was killing it.

The reprieve lands as a growing number of Tesla’s own fans push back on the decision, and on what it says about Tesla’s future as a firm that sells cars to people.

It has been revealed that on November 6, Musk said Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at Giga Texas “around the middle of next year” to make room for Cybercab. On November 9, he wrote the line would shut “in about 8 months” and that Tesla would “have to return deposits for a lot of people.” Now it’s the end of summer.

In order to work through more of the Cybertruck order backlog, production will be extended through the end of summer 2027.

Sources indicate that the reasons have moved around just as much. First it was factory space, then “a very limited number of smart, dedicated people,” then the “opportunity cost” of the truck’s complexity. We went through each of them: Tesla is ending the Cybertruck as sales stall at about 10% of blueprint, Musk’s demand claim doesn’t survive the numbers, and Musk admitted Tesla doesn’t have the talent to run more than one vehicle program.

And the “backlog” is one Tesla built itself. Before the announcement, the truck was selling at a pace of roughly 30,000 units a year, about 10% of the 250,000 Tesla planned for, on a line with over 125,000 units of installed capacity. Telling people the truck is going away creates a last-call rush. That’s not demand Tesla was missing before.

In a recent development, tesla also raised Cybertruck prices by up to 10% the same day and paused orders for the base Dual Motor. The cheapest Cybertruck you can order is now $92,490, up from $69,990 in early August.

Some of the people in that backlog have been waiting a while. Several cheering in Musk’s replies say they’re still waiting on the $59,990 Cybertruck Tesla sold for “10 days only” in February. One asked whether Tesla will prioritize Premium and Cyberbeast orders over theirs. Musk didn’t answer.

The most telling replies weren’t about the truck. Chuck Cook, one of the best-known FSD testers in the Tesla community, quote-tweeted Musk asking him to “change your mind,” adding: “Cybercab won’t haul my bees.”.

Another longtime Tesla supporter, Phil Trubey, asked for “a vehicle roadmap post end of summer 2027,” followed by: “Will Tesla make any other vehicle?”.

In a recent development, that’s the right question, and Tesla hasn’t announced a single latest consumer vehicle to answer it. Tesla started 2026 with five consumer vehicle programs: Model S, Model X, Model 3, Model Y, and Cybertruck. It ended Model S and Model X production in the spring, citing “autonomy.” The Cybertruck goes next. By fall 2027, Tesla’s consumer lineup will be the Model 3 and Model Y, two vehicles that released in 2017 and 2020.

In a recent development, tesla’s answer to the affordable car it promised for years was stripped-down “Standard” versions of those same two vehicles. In China, its second-biggest market, Tesla turned Giga Shanghai into an export hub, and domestic retail sales crashed 66% in October to the lowest level in over four years.

Sources indicate that even Unplugged Performance, the biggest Tesla tuner around, offered to take the Cybertruck line off Tesla’s hands and pay a license fee. People want this truck built. Tesla doesn’t.

We’ve been warning about this for years, and for years we got called haters for it.

Sources indicate that the pattern has been clear since Tesla swapped its affordable car looks for Robotaxi in 2024. No new consumer platform. Model S and X killed “for autonomy.” Cybertruck killed “for Cybercab.” A Roadster pitched as a thruster stunt nine years after its unveiling. Every product decision points away from selling cars to people and toward robotaxis and Optimus, two businesses that don’t generate meaningful revenue today.

I am beginning to suspect that Elon does not always tell the truth.

As long as we have an economic climate that allows massive amounts of money to be made off of speculation as opposed to actual product, future bots and robotaxis have a great deal of value whether they actually become viable or not.

A two-to-three-month extension doesn’t change any of that. It’s a gesture to the loudest part of the fan base, and it happens to let Tesla sell a few thousand more trucks at prices up to 10% higher than last week. Fine. But the people who bought into Tesla’s mission to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy are now realizing that mission was quietly rewritten, and the word “sustainable” didn’t make the cut.

According to recent reports, tesla is becoming a tech giant that sells two aging EVs to fund a bet on autonomy. That might work out for shareholders. We have our doubts, given Tesla is still behind Waymo by every public metric. But it’s a lot less exciting for the people who wanted the next great Tesla car.

The question for fans now: when the Model 3 and Model Y get their own “opportunity cost” post on X, will anyone actually be surprised?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

BYD is apologizing after a supplier error left some owners of its fresh full-size flagship SUV with the wrong wheels.

The Great Tang, or Da Tang as it’s called in China, is the first flagship D-segment SUV under its Dynasty series, the largest and most luxurious SUV from the lineup.

After opening preorders at the Beijing Auto Show in April, BYD said the high-end SUV secured over 30,000 preorders in 24 hours. Two weeks later, preorders reached over 100,000.

By the time it went on sale in mid-June, over 150,000 buyers had preordered the Great Tang, marking a new record for a single BYD model.

While it has been the top-selling pure electric large SUV for two months, with more than 10,000 sold since it hit the market, BYD issued an apology on November 11 for fitting the wrong front and rear wheel rims on some Great Tang models.

The apology comes after several owners complained that the wheels were improperly installed on their vehicles.

BYD stated the matter stemmed from a coding error by the wheel mesh assembly supplier, which led to incorrect assembly on some Great Tang vehicles.

In a recent development, the company mentioned it “immediately” released an investigation and corrected the matter so newly built vehicles will not be affected. In addition, the supplier introduced a fresh visual error-prevention mechanism to limit problems like this going forward.

BYD said the glitch does not affect the vehicle’s handling or pose a safety risk during driving.

Recent findings suggest that the company said owners can take affected vehicles to their local service center for a free inspection and professional wheel rim replacement. It’s also offering a replacement vehicle or compensation for transportation expenses.

Effective immediately, BYD said, the warranty on affected Great Tang vehicles will also be restarted.

Industry observers note that the Great Tang is on sale in China in pure electric (EV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains. The cheapest Premium EV variant starts at 239,900 yuan ($35,500).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries. While the base Premium model uses a 105.79 kWh battery, the Flagship EV trim uses a larger 130.15 kWh battery that delivers up to 590 miles (950 km) of CLTC range. It starts at 269,900 yuan ($40,000).

The Great Tang is huge, measuring 5,263 mm long, 1,999 mm wide, and 1,800 mm high, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm.

In comparison, that’s bigger than the Hyundai IONIQ 9 and Kia EV9. It’s closer in size to the Li Auto L9.

It has been revealed that based on a 1,000V architecture with BYD’s Flash Charging tech, the electric SUV can charge from 10% to 70% in five minutes. For a full recharge, or to go from 10% to 97%, it takes just nine minutes.

After launching in China, BYD executive vice president Stella Li noted the flagship SUV will go on sale in Europe and other overseas markets by the end of 2026 or early 2027.

#64205. Tech Report: I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1654 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: I Tried Adding 10 Minutes of Daily Mobility to My Routine for Two Weeks. Here’s How My Body—And Mind—Changed

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1654 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort.
  • Sources indicate that mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk.
  • It has been revealed that this style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in my early 30s, which means staying fit requires more of a conscious, consistent effort. The natural loss of lean muscle mass and skin elasticity that occurs at this stage of life makes me more mindful of my body and overall well-being. So, I’ve declared this my year of wellness. As part of it, I have been working on adding small bouts of movement that manageably fit into my daily life. Mobility work felt like one of the best ways to do that.

Sources indicate that mobility is an incredibly underrated training modality, yet it’s an essential part of healthy aging—especially for those like me who spend most of the day sitting at a desk. Mobility training focuses on controlled, active movement through a joint’s full range of motion, states Matthew Cifelli, PT, DPT, CSCS, of Attain Physical Therapy.

It has been revealed that this style of movement helps you perform nearly every daily task, from climbing stairs and getting up from a seated position to walking with a full stride and turning your head while driving. But as you age or spend extended periods of time being sedentary, it’s common for muscles to tighten, joints to stiffen, and movement to become less efficient.

“Limited mobility forces the body to compensate with inefficient patterns, increasing the risk of pain, balance issues, and injury,” indicates Cifelli. Maintaining mobility, on the other hand, “supports independence, joint health, and the ability to move confidently through life.”.

It has been revealed that that’s why I recently decided to add just 10 minutes of mobility work to my daily routine for two weeks. Here’s exactly what I did—and how my body changed.

In a recent development, mobility is “not just about ‘feeling loose,’” indicates Cifelli. “It's about teaching the body to use its flexibility in real movement.” It’s a mix of static stretching and flexibility work that focuses on muscle length. “Mobility training targets how well a joint moves and how well you control that motion, which requires coordinated muscle activation and joint stability.”.

It has been revealed that and just a few minutes a day of mobility work can help boost circulation, lubricate the joints, alleviate muscle tension, and improve confidence in daily movement. “Even short sessions, when done daily, create meaningful cumulative change,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, my routine included a combination of exercises and hold times I learned from Portia Page, CPT, in addition to a couple of stretches my physical therapist recommended incorporating into my home regimen. I performed each exercise for one minute, one time through.

During the first week of my experiment, I eased into my 10-minute mobility routine. I was eager to see how it could help improve my “desk body,” a.k.a. tight hips, tense hamstrings, and lower back and neck tension.

I did the workout every morning around 8 a.m. before diving into the madness of the day. It was pretty seamless to add to my mornings, since I have a dedicated workout space in my home, though the routine doesn’t require much space or equipment. Plus, I’m someone who craves routine. Sticking to the same time each morning made this fitness habit sustainable.

Industry observers note that from the get-go, it was clear my body was tense and in desperate need of some stretching and mobility work. My legs, back, and hips all felt stiff at the beginning of the workout. Certain exercises, like the standing forward fold, hip flexor stretch, and supine figure-four stretch were more challenging than the rest. For example, during the first week, I found it difficult to touch the floor when doing the forward fold, so I didn’t force it.

By the end of each session, my body was definitely a bit more relaxed, but I knew I needed to stick with mobility work for more than just a week or two in order to achieve meaningful, lasting results.

I was a dancer growing up, and my body was much more flexible then than it is now. While the Pilates classes I attend three to four times a week have definitely helped me stretch and strengthen my body, a dedicated mobility routine felt like exactly what the doctor ordered. I didn’t realize it would help me in my classes, too. By the end of week one, I felt I was able to move through a more seamless range of motion in certain Pilates exercises like the mermaid and the straight-back hinge on the short box.

Heading into week two, I found myself looking forward to my morning mobility session. It started to feel like more of a natural segue into my day, similar to brushing my teeth, taking my vitamins, or getting dressed. Once I wrapped up stretching and sat down at my desk, my body felt more limber and relaxed as I started work. However, after a couple hours of sitting, I felt much more tense again. The experiment taught me to be mindful of that: My body needs movement throughout the day—not just first thing in the morning.

I felt inspired by this healthy mobility habit and how great I feel afterward, so I wanted to keep the momentum going. During week two, I started building other healthy habits, like getting up to walk around my kitchen and living room every hour and going on a longer brisk walk at the end of the day. Both helped me stay limber throughout the day, rather than just in the morning. My hope is that, with all of these bouts of movement combined, sitting won’t undo all of the wonderful benefits I get from my stretching routine.

Industry observers note that by the end of the second week, I was pleased that my body felt more accustomed to the dedicated mobility work than it had during week one. The more challenging stretches also became slightly easier, which made me feel like I was making genuine progress.

According to recent reports, the routine became a no-brainer—a staple, if you will—in my morning routine: I’d wake up, brew a soothing latte, and get to work on my yoga mat. It also sparked the desire to get up and move more during the workday rather than remain hunched over my laptop for an extended period of time.

Recent findings suggest that because I experienced the tension-relieving benefits of this mobility work almost immediately after each session during week two, I’m now inspired to do it at both the start and end of my day. It’s a great way to ease any built-up stiffness after a long day at my desk before slipping into bed.

Recent findings suggest that that said, one thing I’d love to continue working on is my posture. I didn’t experience any groundbreaking improvements during this two-week timeframe, but I’m hopeful that I’ll make progress down the line. I’m also curious to see whether being consistent with this mobility routine long-term will help my body—especially my hips and lower back—feel less stiff after sitting or lounging for longer periods.

Industry observers note that consistency is key. As with any workout, consistency is essential for success. But alas, it’s something I’ve struggled with over the years. Hectic work weeks filled with deadlines and appointments typically push my fitness to the back burner.

However, during this two-week test period, I was incredibly determined to carve out 10 minutes each day for my stretching regimen, and I’m so glad I did. Sticking with this fitness habit helped me feel better mentally and physically. My body started to feel more flexible and limber by the end of the two-week period—something I don’t think I would have experienced if I were inconsistent with my efforts.

Try this 15-minute mobility routine.

In a recent development, according to Page, a mere 5 to 10 minutes a day of mobility work can make a noticeable difference over time if you’re consistent with the habit. She recommends thinking of stretching “not as a luxury but as basic maintenance for your body—like brushing your teeth.”.

According to recent reports, kickstarting the day with fitness can promote other healthy habits. Starting the day with mobility work inspired me to follow other healthy habits throughout. After all, I was already off to a solid start and wanted to keep that momentum going strong.

It has been revealed that following each mobility session, I felt accomplished, energized, and ready to tackle the day. I found myself sticking with my regular Pilates workouts, making all-around healthier meal choices, snacking less, and adding brief “movement snacks” to my afternoons to break up the time spent sitting at my desk.

Industry observers note that mobility is a low-barrier starting point for movement. What I love best about this mobility workout? I don’t need to leave the comfort of my home or have access to fancy equipment. I’ve seamlessly incorporated these exercises into my self-care routine, and it just takes 10 minutes of my morning before I dive into work deadlines and commitments.

While there’s always room for improvement—and I’d like to add even more stretches to my routine—I felt incredibly accomplished overall with only a 10-minute routine. I’m hopeful that, by starting now and being consistent with mobility training, I can help prepare my body to tackle everyday tasks with ease. This training can also help me stay mobile, confident, and independent in my adventurous lifestyle for the long term.

The Kids Are Outside: The Rise of the Adult Children’s ADU

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home.
  • While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.
  • Recent findings suggest that blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Diane and Steve Weaver of Castro Valley, California, shipped their son Sam off to college in 2013, they hoped he’d someday find his dream job and a nice home. And while Sam is thriving professionally as a sales rep with his own place, they never expected that his house would be in their backyard. But the nightmarish Bay Area real estate market made a 400-square-foot ADU (accessory dwelling unit) on his parents’ property, complete with a separate entrance and direct street access, seem like the best option for the 32-year-old. “It was becoming difficult for him to afford rent while also saving toward eventually buying a place of his own,” Diane tells AD. “He’s close by, but it really feels like he has his own home.”.

While in-law suites and granny flats (a nickname for when ADUs house in-laws) have become popular among young, successful homeowners who want their elderly parents nearby, a growing number of Americans are now adding ADUs to their properties to house adult children threatening to move back in and reverse their status as empty nesters.

Diane and Steve Weaver on their property’s ADU.

Recent findings suggest that blame the return of the flock on the home affordability crisis. These days a homebuyer needs an annual income between $110,000 and $113,000—well above the national average income of $64,220 per year—to comfortably afford a median-priced home in the US, which is presently priced at $434,900. While this has led some grown kids to move back into their childhood bedrooms, in cases where acreage allows, families like the Weavers are opting to be neighbors instead of housemates by setting up self-contained living spaces on the same lot as their single-family homes. In California, they’re certainly no outlier. The state has passed legislation specifically encouraging the construction of ADUs to address the housing shortage—which resulted in quadruple the number of ADU permits issued in the Golden State from 2017 to 2022.

Those in the ADU construction game say families like the Weavers make up an increasingly large slice of their business. Jeremy Nova, co-founder of the Colorado-based prefab ADU builder Studio Home, says ADUs for adult children are popular among his clients because the arrangement is mutually beneficial. The kids are afforded some independence and the ability to save money, “while for the parents, it can also be a long-term investment. The same space that houses an adult child today could eventually become a rental or a separate living space for a caregiver.” ADU builders on the opposite coast are seeing the same demand. Justin Olewack, president of Bolt Builders, says that ADUs for adult children are becoming a top request among his clientele in the DC, Virginia, and Maryland areas, where housing costs have risen 61 percent since 2016.

If it cuts costs and results in a sellable amenity down the line, perhaps moving back home isn’t the failure-to-launch scenario it was once seen as.

An ADU by Studio Home, built in the backyard of a Scottsdale, Arizona, family’s property.

Sources indicate that once a family’s adult child moves out of the property’s ADU, especially if it has a kitchen and bathroom, the structure can serve as a rental, providing passive income for retired parents. Tracy Noh, who hired John Brennan of BZBuild Co to build her daughter Eliza Bowen an ADU in Burbank, was thinking long-term with her compound planning. “An in-home apartment would require sharing the space of our 1,000-square-foot main home. And, as someone who works from home, the ADU seemed a better solution,” she states.

Noh and Eliza show off their Burbank ADU.

The living arrangement has also enabled Noh and her daughter to develop their own life paths. The structure gives her daughter a space in which she can become a young adult, and Noh the opportunity to step back from making the day-to-day household decisions. The former is learning how to manage her own household: planning meals, budgeting expenses, and making time for household chores.

“That change in dynamic also allows us both to remain much calmer in our interactions with each other,” Noh says. It’s not just because there’s a separate place for each of them to retreat to; Noh says she has “gained an enormous amount of respect for Eliza and her ability to manage her own home. It’s a fabulous opportunity to begin to build that adult-to-adult relationship with your child.”.

The interior of Tracy Noh’s ADU by BZBuild Co.

Industry observers note that while modest ADUs serve single occupants just fine, more sizable ADUs allow a family’s adult children to bring their own kids in tow. Oren Amir, co-founder of SoCal builder GO Home Builders, points out that in his experience, the catalyst for aging parents to build an ADU for their adult children is almost never just the adult child themselves: It’s the grandchild they will be bringing with them. “The call comes a few months before or after a baby arrives,” he notes. The grandparents don’t want to travel to visit their grandkids; they want them living nearby. Rent in Los Angeles is what stops people from saving, and early parenthood is when saving matters most, Amir says. An ADU in a grandparent’s backyard, therefore, lets the adult children stay in the neighborhood, raise the baby near help, and set some money aside for when the time comes to leave the nest for good. “Everyone gets what they need and nobody has to move in,” Amir says of the arrangement.

While the Weaver family ADU is Sam’s for now, it could grow up to be a granny flat someday. “It’s possible that Sam might live in the main house and we could move into the ADU as we age,” says Diane. “It gives us a lot of options for how the space can be used as our family’s needs change.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Anthropic mathematician indicates Claude helped him crack the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old puzzle with a $1 million prize attached.

His claim surfaced Friday, one day after the AI tech giant’s stock-market debut, and has not yet been independently verified.

It has been revealed that “I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,” Levent Alpöge wrote in a four-page note. He says the method also resolves the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, which extends the question to other mathematical functions.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

According to recent reports, alpöge says he and Claude encoded their argument in Lean, software used to check mathematical proofs step by step. His note links to 14 downloadable parts of the proof archive, but its availability does not amount to acceptance by the mathematical community.

According to recent reports, alpöge states he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about a possible announcement “late Sunday night,” November 15. He then consulted tech giant leadership and mentioned there was a constraint to respect, without explaining precisely what it was.

In a recent development, “The precise timing is horrible,” he acknowledged. Alpöge rejected a cynical interpretation of the timing, but did not explicitly say the manufacturer’s IPO caused the delay.

Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday, November 19, after raising $81.34 billion in its offering.

Industry observers note that alpöge figured in September’s AI math wars. OpenAI claimed it had solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem as he and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster pursued related fluid-equation work, sparking a credit dispute over research priority.

Recent findings suggest that openAI followed in October with 722 manuscripts generated by an unreleased model, grouped into 372 families of results. Only 162 included Lean-checked main results, and mathematicians demanded stronger evidence rather than accepting the organization’s flood of claims at face value.

It has been revealed that some mathematicians fear a “mathocalypse,” with AI solving coveted problems before researchers can learn from pursuing them. Toronto mathematician Daniel Litt warned that, without adaptation, “there’s just no more math in 50 years.” At an MIT panel this week, Buckmaster argued mathematics still requires human understanding.

Recent findings suggest that first posed by Bernhard Riemann in 1859, the hypothesis predicts where certain zeros of the Riemann zeta function fall. The question matters because those zeros are linked to the distribution of prime numbers, whose patterns underlie extensive mathematical research.

A proof would be a historic mathematical result, since experts have been trying to solve that for over a century.

Lean can verify that formal deductions obey its rules. Mathematicians still need to reproduce the archive, check the formalized theorem matches the original conjecture, and examine the claimed result before considering it settled.

Anthropic previously reported progress on the zeta function without claiming to solve the full hypothesis. Alpöge’s newly introduced assertion goes far beyond that earlier work.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists the Riemann hypothesis among its Millennium Prize Problems, each carrying a $1 million award. Under the institute’s prize rules, a proposed solution must be published in a qualifying outlet, survive at least two years of scrutiny, and earn general acceptance before the prize can be considered.

  • This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kia became the first non-European brand to score a hat trick at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, Germany’s most prestigious auto awards.

The Korean automaker won a triple crown at the 2026 Golden Steering Wheel Awards, with the EV2, K4 Sportswagon, and EV5 taking first in their class.

This is the first time a non-European brand has won three Golden Steering Wheel Awards in a single year in the prestigious award’s 50-year history.

The award is organized by AUTO BILD and BILD am SONNTAG with 90 new models nominated this year. Readers chose 27 finalists, three in each of the nine classes, which were then tested by a panel of celebrities and auto experts.

Industry observers note that the judges tested the vehicles at the DEKRA-Lausitzring racetrack. Vehicles were judged on handling, comfort, ease of use, quality, and everyday practicality, as well as the sustainability and value they offer.

Kia won across three very different categories with the fully electric EV2 and EV5, alongside the gas-powered K4 Sportswagon.

The EV2, Kia’s entry-level electric SUV, won the award for the “Best Car Under €30,000.” Developed specifically for Europe, the compact EV is only 4.06 meters long, but offers up to 403 liters of cargo space.

It also offers a WLTP driving range of up to 453 km (281 miles), which is among the longest in its class.

In a recent development, kia’s EV5 beat out the Audi Q3 and Cupra Formentor VZ5 in the compact SUV category. Introduced in December, the EV5 is about the size of the Sportage.

It’s available with front- and all-wheel-drive powertrains and offers a range of over 550 km (341 miles). Depending on the configuration, the EV5 can tow up to 1,800 kg (about 4,000 lbs).

Lastly, the Kia K4 Sportswagon, launched in May, outperformed the fresh Volkswagen ID.3 Neo and Cupra Born in the compact class.

In Europe, Kia offers a full lineup of all-electric vehicles, from the entry-level EV2 to the EV3, EV4, EV5, EV6, three-row EV9, and PV5 van.

Industry observers note that sadly, Kia has no prepares to sell the EV2 or EV5 in the US, but its popular EV3 (see our review) is now available. In 2024, the Kia EV3 won the Golden Steering Wheel award for “Best Car under €40,000.”.

The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $29,890, making it among the most affordable EVs in the US. It’s available in five trims and two battery packs.

The base Kia EV3 Light has a 58.3 kWh battery that provides up to 221 miles of range, while the Wind, Land, GT-Line, and GT use an 81.4 kWh battery for up to 321 miles of range.

Get the Women’s Health Beginner Workout Initiative: 4-Week Strength Training and Cardio Program

📅 23 Feb 2023 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately.
  • So, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party.
  • Industry observers note that the Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s not just you—everyone really is starting to work out lately. My feed is full of people hitting the weights for the first time ever or setting major goals like getting their first pull-up. And let me just say: It’s awesome!

So, if that’s you, let me officially say welcome to the party. When you’re starting to work out, it can be hard to sift through all the options and find a program that’s actually accessible for a true beginner (or, someone restarting after quite some time). That is, until now.

Industry observers note that the Women’s Health+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan takes the guesswork out of starting your fitness journey. This comprehensive program guides you through strength and cardio workouts that only take between 20 and 45 minutes. And, of course, it answers every burning question you could have about starting a fitness routine.

It has been revealed that no matter your age or experience, starting an exercise routine has many benefits, notes Kristen McParland, CPT, your coach for the next four weeks. Building muscle increases total-body strength; your bones, ligaments, and tendons get healthier; and even your blood pressure and immunity may improve. So lace up those sneakers and we’ll see you at the gym now, too.

Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Plan.

Over the next four weeks, you’ll follow a specific initiative each day, focusing either on strength training, optional cardio, active recovery, or rest (more on these, below). Each strength workout includes a warm-up and a cooldown (which you can use on cardio days, too). More info on each below.

In a recent development, simply follow the instructions of each full-body strength training workout in the Women's Health+ Beginner Workout Proposal. You can find detailed how-to instructions for each exercise in the Exercise Guide section of the PDF.

Equipment Needed: Dumbbells, kettlebells, a step or box, and a slam ball. Don’t have access to a kettlebell or slam ball? Don't worry—you can still do those exercises with a dumbbell.

Industry observers note that cardio is key for everyone, regardless of fitness level or routine. That’s because when you’re lifting heavy, your heart needs to be able to take on that stress. Training cardio—through running, cycling, or brisk walking—will help improve your heart strength.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Complete 20 to 30 minutes of running, biking, cycling, rowing, or using the elliptical or stair climber (whatever you enjoy). No matter which form of cardio you choose, start with interval training: exert yourself for 30 seconds, then go at a light pace for 1 to 2 minutes, alternating the pattern for a total of 20 minutes. The goal is to “get your heart rate up, but then pull it back and recover,” McParland claims. Eventually, you’ll be able to decrease the rest time and maintain that higher-intensity movement for 15 to 20 minutes without a break.

Recent findings suggest that your activity on this day is up to you. The goal is to do some kind of low-intensity movement lasting 20 minutes. Some ideas: outdoor walk or hike, bike ride, incline treadmill walk, yoga, or Pilates class.

Recent findings suggest that take this day to relax so your muscles have time to repair. Still, if your body is craving some type of activity for recovery, you could stretch, go for a walk, or even try a treatment like a massage, sauna, or cold-plunge session.

Here’s how things will progress each week.

According to recent reports, complete the five programmed workouts when it’s convenient for you. Focus on your form and take your two rest days when you need to recover.

If you completed all the workouts in Week 1, repeat them during Week 2, adjusting one variable in your routine, McParland notes: the number of reps or sets, the weight, the speed of the moves (slower is harder). If you missed a workout, don’t stress. Refocus on completing all of the Week 1 workouts before making any of the changes above.

You’ve officially done two full weeks of this workout strategy—nice job! During this third week, repeat the workouts from Week 2 in exactly the same way or adjust one variable again (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, and rest periods). If you feel you’re crushing it and are ready to level up, try the third full-body strength workout.

It has been revealed that still going strong? Thought so! Hit all six workouts and adjust one variable per workout for an extra challenge (reps or sets, weight, range of motion, speed, rest time). You can also ramp up your cardio time (to 30 to 40 minutes) or speed, shorten rest intervals (for interval training), or raise your step goal by 10 percent (e.g., if your daily step goal was 5,000 a day, make it 5,500).

Ready to become your strongest self? Download the WH+ 4-Week Beginner Workout Initiative now.

When you’re just beginning to work out, do a minimum of two full-body strength training days each week, McParland recommends. During both of those days, you should hit at least one exercise from each category of the foundational movement patterns. This will give you enough of a challenge to stimulate muscle growth, she states.

During the first two weeks of this blueprint, you will have two strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will 20 to 30 minutes), one day of active rest (a stint of low-intensity movement lasting at least 20 minutes), and two recovery days, for a total of five workouts per week.

Industry observers note that after those two weeks, see how your body feels and if your body is craving a third day of full-body training. If so, progress to the next phase of this strategy. That weekly schedule consists of three strength training days per week (each session will run 36 to 43 minutes), two optional cardio/step days per week (each session will run 20 to 30 minutes), one active rest day (lasting at least 20 minutes), and one recovery day, for a total of six workouts per week. If your body isn’t ready for three strength-training days yet, wait another two weeks. Once you’ve completed the full four weeks of this plan, consider adding in the third day.

What kind of weights should I choose?

Start with medium weights that will challenge you for 10 to 12 reps, notes Sariya. Essentially, you’ll want to feel you’ve reached 70 to 80 percent of your rate of perceived exertion (i.e., your fatigue level is at a 7 or 8 out of 10) by the time you’re doing your final reps in a set. When you feel you can do more than 12 reps, it’s time to increase your weight, but keep the same number of reps. This way, you’re always working toward your goal of building strength.

As for how much to increase by: a good rule of thumb is 2.5 to 5 pounds for an upper-body exercise and 5 to 10 pounds for a lower-body move.

What if I need to rest in the middle of a set?

Resting during a workout is important—if you don’t take enough time to recover between exercises, you won’t have enough energy in your body for the next one. With this proposal, you’ll rest between moves in a superset or tri-set for 20 to 30 seconds, or however long it takes to transition between exercises. Between supersets and tri-sets, you’ll rest for one minute.

It has been revealed that if you get fatigued in the middle of a set, push through if you feel safe doing so, Sariya notes. However, if you feel dizzy or fear you might drop a weight on yourself, put it down and take time to recover. When you’re feeling better, you can start again. If you’re in any sort of pain, stop the workout entirely.

What kind of cardio should I do?

Cardio is a great supplement to strength training, McParland says. Plus, it has a slew of benefits, such as better endurance in strength training, better blood pressure regulation, and higher VO2 max, she says.

If you’re a beginner when it comes to cardio, simply start at your own pace and build. Pick any form of cardio you enjoy, whether that’s brisk walking, running, cycling, or swimming, and sprinkle it in two or three days a week for 20 to 30 minutes, McParland recommends.

What should I do on recovery days?

In a recent development, on an active rest day, you’ll still exercise a bit through low-intensity movement, like a leisurely bike ride or hike. On a recovery day, you’ll do just that: recover. After all, you need to give your muscles time to rebuild and repair, Sariya notes. But to maximize the recovery aspect, you can also opt to stretch, go for a gentle walk, or even get a self-care body treatment like a massage.

In a recent development, once you’ve got the WH+ Beginner Workout Plan under your belt, you’re ready to take things to another level. One way to do that is by simply restarting the program—and completing the moves with heavier weights this time. (This is called progressive overload, and it’s another foundational concept in strength training. The idea is that over time, you will keep increasing the stimulus to your muscles to continuously challenge them and make them stronger.).

Industry observers note that picking the right weight is an art as much as it is a science, but for a general rule of thumb, for upper-body moves, increase your weights by 2.5 to 5 pounds and see how that feels. For lower-body ones, try adding 5 to 10. You should feel like you’re ending each set two to three reps away from failure (where your form starts to break down). You can tell you’re close if your range of motion starts to shorten or your reps are slowing down. That’s how you know you’re successfully challenging yourself. And, if you don’t happen to have a lot of different-sized weights at your disposal, you can always just increase the number of reps you do instead.

But, if you’re looking for something newly introduced, WH+ has a bunch of other trainer-created programs to help you grow your knowledge and confidence in the gym and attack other fitness goals.
