Menopause Was a Hushed Conversation—Until Gen X Changed Everything

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1564 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause.
  • It has been revealed that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle.
  • Industry observers note that these discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that sharon Cancio, 28, didn’t grow up knowing much about menopause. She didn’t learn anything about it in school, nor from the women in her family. But when she was a teenager, she started noticing her mother’s mood shifting. Around her mid-to-late 40s, “she became much snappier, more easily irritated, and sometimes just seemed angry in a way that felt completely different from the mom I remembered growing up,” she recalls. “I genuinely thought life had simply worn her down.”.

It has been revealed that cancio didn’t start connecting the dots until she came off birth control at 25 and noticed how dramatically her own mood changed around her cycle. Once she realized her mother had entered perimenopause, she went down an internet rabbit hole to learn about it. Women were discussing—in detail—what was happening to their bodies on TikTok and Reddit. Some women were going through menopause early, others were seeking answers for their symptoms.

Industry observers note that these discussions are a far cry from what conversations around menopause used to look like: nonexistent. In the past, there wasn’t much education—or even real discussion—on what happens to the female body after 40, forcing women to hustle through hot flashes and mood swings behind closed doors.

In a recent development, but within the last few years, there’s been a shift: Gen X women are the first to go through this hormonal transition in the age of social media—and they’re not afraid to talk about their experiences, claims Gillan Goddard, MD, an endocrinologist and an adjunct assistant professor of medicine at the NYU Langone Hospital. They’re educating an entire generation of younger women in the process. Posts about brain fog, inconsistent sleep patterns, and unfamiliar-feeling bodies have become the first real health literacy that this generation’s daughters, Gen Zers, have gotten about their own hormonal futures. These small conversations have significant implications when it comes to learning more about their future health.

Industry observers note that the lack of menopause education starts in classrooms: Almost all U.S. states require teenagers to learn about puberty, reproductive health, and sexual disease prevention through sex education classes. But the content and depth of those classes may not favor women’s health: A 2024 study in the Journal of School Health looked at the state of menstrual health education in U.S. K-12 public schools. Researchers analyzed the education standards from each state’s Department of Education site, searching terms like “menstruation,” “menopause,” “period,” “reproduction,” and “puberty.” It found that menstrual health education—especially menopause—is profoundly rare.

Industry observers note that there’s also a lack of menopause education in medical schools. Only 31.3 percent of U.S. ob-gyn residency programs include a menopause curriculum, according to a 2023 study in Menopause. The result resembles a serious disconnect: The transition affects nearly half of the population, but the majority of the doctors tasked with treating menopause have received almost no training on how to do it.

Menopause just isn’t prioritized during residency training. Instead, the “focus during training was placed on surgical skills and labor and delivery responsibilities, both considered more urgent and time-consuming,” says Alyssa Dweck, MD, chief medical officer of Bonafide Health and a Menopause Society Certified Practitioner located in New York City. Ob-gyns can earn certifications in (peri)menopause, from organizations including the Menopause Society and Integrative Women’s Health Institute—but they’re not required. Clinicians should have more comprehensive training in medical school and beyond, says Dr. Dweck. But there should also be more funding and resources for women’s health research for treatment options.

Industry observers note that when doctors aren’t familiar with menopause, “mood changes, cognitive changes, and body aches are often misunderstood or ignored,” says Dr. Goddard. This can lead to misdiagnoses, and to women not receiving proper treatment for symptoms caused by menopause. This is pretty common: A 2025 survey conducted by health care company Biote of over 1,000 women ages 30 to 60 in the U.S. found that 39 percent of women have been misdiagnosed and prescribed medication by a provider for conditions like depression.

Sources indicate that tikTok and Instagram have filled the menopause education void in the U.S. Conversations about life in menopause have spread awareness about what the condition is actually like, crushing stigmas. This visibility is not only helping younger viewers learn what they can expect later in life—it’s also helping mothers start more health-forward conversations with their daughters.

Milan Parker, 25, has always had open conversations about health with her mom. “She’s always been really honest with me about what she’s going through, even the more personal parts that people sometimes consider taboo,” she says. But social media increased this dynamic tenfold: Parker’s mother underwent a hysterectomy due to fibroids at 48, which made her enter early menopause. Following the surgery, her mother joined a menopause support group on Facebook. “Seeing that there were women all across the country going through similar things made her more open to talking to me about it,” Parker says.

For instance, Parker’s mom finally explained how debilitating her hot flashes really were. (She’d stopped going on trips with her because she was embarrassed about looking sweaty.) “There were times when I thought maybe my mom just didn’t want to go out with me,” she notes. “I’m really grateful that she made it something we could actually talk about instead of something that had to stay a secret.”.

For daughters, it can be hard to watch their mothers struggle in menopause and not know how to help, but the experience can also help them grow closer. “The emotional experience can be a mix of empathy, grief, anxiety, and closeness,” says Ashley Peña, LCSW, a clinical social worker and the vice president of outpatient operations at Mission Connection.

Even though Cancio’s mom didn’t tell her when she was going through menopause, the experience helped her gain compassion for her mother and better understand her own body. “As a teenager, I honestly thought she was just becoming grumpy or ‘getting old,’ which I feel terrible admitting now,” she indicates. “As an adult woman, I have so much more empathy.”.

Recent findings suggest that having a raw look at what menopause is actually like—whether through a screen or a conversation with their mother—shapes how younger women view aging and how to prepare themselves for what’s ahead. Hearing that they may one day inevitably experience sleepless nights, sudden anger, brain fog, and the loss of identity can be scary, to say the least. But “open conversation about menopause helps women hear the full scope of menopause experiences and how women dealt effectively with their symptoms,” Dr. Goddard says. It can make the condition sound less scary to younger women.

In fact, growing conversations around menopause can actually inspire younger women to learn about it earlier. “I am seeing patients of all ages, Gen Z included, who have become more inquisitive and engaged in their health overall,” Dr. Dweck indicates. Some of her young patients have told her they’ve already started talking to their older relatives about menopause and hormone health. They’re also more open about discussing fertility and egg freezing.

Industry observers note that even though menopause is now common dinner table conversation, the root of the (non-communication) concern still needs to be fixed. “The only way we normalize talking about women’s health is by talking about it,” Cancio states. “Ask questions, stay curious, and don’t be afraid to learn from women who have already been through it.”.

It has been revealed that mothers going through (peri)menopause can have a series of casual conversations about it with their kids. (The earlier, the better.) They can keep the conversation casual and tailored to the child’s developmental age. For instance, moms with children under the age of 13 can briefly mention that they’re “going through a body change.” Then, as the kids get older, they can talk more openly about what they’re experiencing, says Dr. Dweck. Encouraging their children to ask questions about menopause can also build empathy and normalize conversations surrounding health.

On the flip side, Parker wants Gen Z women to pay attention to what their mothers are going through, and not wait until the right moment to spark a conversation. “Having those conversations with my mom has made that feel a lot less scary and a lot more human,” she claims. “Every stage of life comes sooner than you think, so it’s worth paying attention to your health long before you feel like you have to.”.

It has been revealed that cancio didn’t feel like she could have those conversations with her mom, which is part of what inspired her to start making content around women’s health topics for younger women. “I started thinking about the girl who was sitting at home Googling something because she was too embarrassed to ask her mom, or the girl who thought something was wrong with her because nobody had ever explained that what she was experiencing was normal,” she says.

In a recent development, even though the way that Gen Z is learning about menopause isn’t perfect—whether through a viral post or their mother—it’s still a step in the right direction. By doing her part, Cancio hopes to have a completely different relationship with her future daughter “where no topic about her body is off limits and she never feels like she has to search for answers alone.”.

Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.
  • UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations.
  • UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

According to recent reports, previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This latest study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

Sources indicate that the researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

Sources indicate that when the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”.

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

In a recent development, these findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd noted.

According to recent reports, judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

In a recent development, she noted that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is crucial to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

Recent findings suggest that “I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” stated Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”.

Canada’s government wants to make it easier for citizens to drive electric, and they’re putting more than $4 billion in funding for electricity infrastructure and grid modernization that includes more than 55,000 upcoming EV chargers.

The proposed federal budget set aside $4 billion (CAD) for grid improvements, with a $~635 million carveout specifically for EV charging infrastructure with $587 million of that set aside to renew the Zero-Emission Vehicle Infrastructure Program (ZEVIP), which funds the development of latest public EV charging stations.

In a recent development, “The charging industry is really encouraged by the multi-year investment in the budget,” explains Travis Allan, president and CEO of the Canadian Charging Infrastructure Council (CCIC) told Electric Autonomy. “We’ll be looking to make sure that we have great programs in place to deal with the barriers faced by people living in condos and apartments, public fast charging, which needs to cover major corridors and metropolitan areas, and then also charging for fleets and medium- and heavy-duty vehicles, which make up a major share of transportation emissions.”.

The rest of the $4 billion will be spent on electricity infrastructure expansion over the next 10 years, starting in 2027 and running through 2036. Because it’s Canada where nearly 60% of electrical generation already comes from renewable hydro and wind power, renewable energy is a de-facto priority, with carveouts for the Smart Renewables and Electrification Pathways Program, latest data and modeling efforts to guide grid planning, and $1.6 billion to modernize power systems in northern and remote communities.

The charging infrastructure program highlighted here, ZEVIP, would help charge point operators by covering up to 50% of eligible project expenses for most projects, and up to 75% of projects led by indigenous developers with caps of up to $2 million per project.

Canada continues to take steps to separate itself from the wild swings and economic chaos caused by America’s random tariffs, trade policies, and dumb oil wars – and building out an infrastructure that makes it easier for its citizens to give affordable Chinese EVs a chance while strengthening its relationship with the US’ biggest economic rival?

Southern Ontario for example is very well covered with fast chargers. But the market is there so companies install them. Northern Ontario, the trans Canada highway needs these chargers badly.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

This is part of the Men's Health Body Bible, a collection of cutting-edge stories focused on helping you build more muscle using the latest science and lessons from some of the finest athletes and trainers on the planet.

In a recent development, THE SECRET TO training your abs is out—and it entails more than situps and planks, more than just targeting your rectus abdominis, the ballyhooed band of muscle between your chest and your hips. If you want true core strength (and, yes, that six-pack), a growing group of experts will tell you that you need to carry heavy weights and walk. This forces your core to constantly microcorrect and rebalance as you move, explains Aaron Horschig, C.S.C.S., D.P.T., a St. Louis–based physical therapist. You also need to twist and turn, challenging your oblique muscles and back extensors.

Sources indicate that “While there’s nothing wrong with training the abs for show, training for stability—which encompasses all of the muscles that surround the spine and hips—is essential training for everyone,” states Horschig. His latest book, Rebuilding Milo, includes a variety of exercises, many of which challenge your entire core—think lower back extensors, glutes, and obliques, which all team up with your abs to stabilize and bolster your back, lending postural support.

Unlike body parts that handle just one or two tasks (like your biceps, which are most heavily utilized to bend your elbows), all those core muscles have a host of responsibilities. They work together to flex your spine (as happens during a classic situp), and they help rotate your shoulders so you can turn to look at a friend. They also prevent excessive rounding of the lower back (known as anti-flexion), a key tactic in the battle to stop back pain. The ideal abs regimen trains all these functions, protecting you against injuries and readying your core (and spine) for anything life can throw at you. Horschig claims people finally get that. “More and more people are starting to understand the true role of core,” he says.

The end result of all this work? A lower back that’s armor-plated against persistent pain, and the ability to move athletically and fluidly. And along the way, you’ll build those six-pack abs, too.

It has been revealed that HOW TO DO IT:An underrated plank upgrade, this move challenges your abs and obliques (and your glutes, too!). Start in pushup position, feet wide. Lift your left hand and touch it to your right shoulder. Keep your hips square as you do. Repeat on the other side.

REPS & SETS:Work for time, not reps, doing three 40-second sets.

It has been revealed that HOW TO DO IT:Stand in a split stance, left shoulder next to the high pulley of a cable machine, both hands grasping the handle, then bend at the knees until your left thigh is nearly parallel to the floor. Keep your hips square to the front as you pull the cable across your body, then return it to the start.

REPS & SETS:Do 10 to 12 reps per side. Do 3 sets.

HOW TO DO IT:Stand holding kettlebells in both hands, the left bell at your chest, the right bell at your hip. Walk forward (or march in place) for 10 to 15 steps per leg. Move slowly, working to keep your hips square.

REPS & SETS:Do 2 sets per side, challenging your abs and lower-back muscles to keep you upright against the heavy load.

TRAIN YOUR ABS EVERYDAY. Some muscle groups require several days to recover, but your core muscles are built to be resilient. That means you can train them nearly every day. Consider doing 3 or 4 sets of core work in every work- out, rotating in new and different ab exercises to continually challenge your rectus abdominis, oblique muscles, and lower-back spinal erectors.

Sources indicate that NEVER GOING HEAVY. Bodyweight planks and situps are a solid starting point for your ab training. But just like any other muscle, core muscles are meant to be loaded and overloaded. Add resistance to your core training, and don’t be afraid to challenge yourself, especially on moves like the mixed-rack carry above. “You have to do that sometimes,” indicates the popular bodybuilder and trainer known as Ulisses Jr. “I’d be lying if I told you I didn’t load my abs.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sheets get slept in every night and washed every week (in theory) which means it doesn’t take long to learn which ones hold up under use. Every retailer here comes recommended by an AD editor or contributor who has lived with the bedding at home for a long stretch: flannel kept on the bed through May, linen hauled to a communal laundromat and back, or a sheet set that survives a dog digging in every night.

It has been revealed that each brand earned its spot for a reason, whether that’s price, a cooling fabric, an unusually wide color range, or embroidery done by hand. Rest assured: they’re all comfy.

In a recent development, for bedding basics that won’t damage the budget, Quince is our first stop. Its European Linen Sheet Set earned our pick for the best affordable linen sheets, and senior shopping editor Nashia Baker has recently added the brand to her list of favorites. “The price point is unbeatable, and I love that they offer bedding sets in beautiful colorways and a variety of fabric options,” she states. “The quality is also impressive, especially considering the affordability.”.

According to recent reports, made from 100% European flax, the sheets cost a fraction of what competitors charge, thanks in part to Quince’s direct-to-consumer model which skips traditional retail markups. “I love its airy nature along with the gorgeous Bordeaux color that complements the rest of my decor,” says Baker. The bedding range extends to quilts and coverlets, , and the brand’s down comforter also made our ranking of the best comforters.

It has been revealed that anyone who has paused a Nancy Meyers movie to study the bedroom should start with Serena & Lily. The brand is based in Sausalito, California, but its textured, breezy bedding and decor would look right at home on any coast, Nantucket included. The range covers lightweight linen and crisp cotton percale in pale colors and easygoing prints.

Of all the bedding Baker has tested, the Nantucket Stripe Sheet Set ranks near the top for its light weight and “worn-in texture,” which keeps the linen soft instead of scratchy. The ruffle trim keeps her bed from looking too plain. “The striped mink print does give a seaside vibe, but it’s been neutral enough to layer with any color bed cover without clashing with the rest of my minimal, romantic decor over the few months I’ve tested the set,” she adds. For a top layer, there’s the scalloped Baywood Quilt, which Alpert likes as a light blanket for “when you want to throw something over while you read your favorite Emily Henry book in bed.”.

Industry observers note that boll & Branch sheets arrive feeling as if they’ve already been through several wash cycles, without the fraying or pilling that usually comes with that. Contributor Rachel Fletcher tested the brand’s percale, Supima cotton, flannel, and linen, but its signature sateen stood out most for its long-staple cotton and a soft, smooth finish. “That extra-soft feel, paired with the lovely, cooling properties, make them feel like the luxury sheets they are,” she claims. Converts can outfit the rest of the room too, with Boll & Branch’s mattresses and bedroom furniture.

Brooklinen started out selling two things, cotton percale and sateen sheets, and has since added cashmere, brushed flannel, and a long list of prints. Pieces come in bundled sets or one at a time, and prices land between the budget brands and the luxury labels. Our editors keep coming back to the linen sheets, which they use in every season.

Recent findings suggest that “Since I don’t live my life on a Greek island, I thought white linen sheets year-round might be a slightly bold move, but the nature of the fiber is versatile and temperature regulating,” says AD contributor Madeleine Luckel, who tested the Core Sheet Set. Fletcher sleeps on the Luxe Sheet Set and credits it with keeping her cool. “I’m a hot sleeper with sensitive skin, and they’re really cool on my skin at night, which is a huge relief,” she says. “I love the breathability of these sheets.”.

Few bedding brands have tied their name to sustainability as closely as Coyuchi. Its linen sheets are made from certified organic French flax grown without synthetic fertilizers or pesticides, and the brand also offers percale, sateen, and flannel sheets. The earthy color palette is a selling point on its own.

“I love the color, which is what drew me to these sheets in the first place,” indicates Sam Cochran, global features editor. “They’re the perfect brown—a tad auburn, ever so slightly timeworn in palette.”.

According to recent reports, shopping writer Julia Harrison and contributor Kate McGregor agree: Garnet Hill is their “secret spot” for bedding. Harrison is devoted to the flannel sheets and admits she leaves them on the bed through May because “they’re so soft, I’d rather suffer in my own sweat than switch them out.” The ticking stripe is “perfectly classic—like a true vintage piece, but not actually vintage…that might be tough sell in the bedding department.” Alpert also loves her flannel pick, a duvet cover that “signals a cottagecore moment without going over the top.” Paired with her Ostermoor duvet insert, it’s “like climbing under a layer of meringue.” Garnet Hill specializes in vintage-inspired designs, patchwork quilts especially, made in 100% linen and 100% cotton options at reasonable prices.

In a recent development, cozy Earth makes breathable bedding for people who run hot at night, and its signature bamboo bedding, made of 100% viscose, are the brand’s best-known example. “I honestly thought these sheets were silk,” indicates contributor Megan Wahn. “That’s how smooth and soft they feel.” Wahn tested them mostly in winter, and despite feeling cool to the touch, they kept her warm. “I’m especially eager to see how they perform in the summer,” she adds. “Something about their smoothness makes me think the summer-night sweats won’t stand a chance.”.

Parachute is where we send anyone after classic, well-made cotton bedding. Its sets and bundles are designed with sustainability in mind, and the percale and brushed cotton are made by artisans at the brand’s factory in Portugal.

Industry observers note that “We love [Parachute] because the bedding is designed to provide a hotel-like experience, offering a perfect balance of softness and crispness,” says Stephanie Kraus of Stephanie Kraus Designs, whose clients favor the brand’s linen bedding sets. “They become softer with each wash while maintaining their durability and are super soft to sleep in every night.”.

It has been revealed that fletcher also praises the brand’s commitment to organic, ethically sourced materials; the Organic Cloud Cotton Duvet Set, for one, is made of Oeko-Tex-certified 100% cotton. “I try a lot of bedding in this line of work and the more I do, the more I appreciate ethical and organic production, even if the price tag is a little higher,” she claims.

It has been revealed that greenRow makes charming, long-lasting bedding from recycled and sustainably sourced materials, and it has won over several people on the Shop AD team. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls the Helena Floral Sheet Set “without a doubt, the softest sheets I own.” She compares the cotton satin to velvet, and the butter-yellow florals and green micro-gingham ruffle make the set prettier still. McGregor, meanwhile, is partial to the reversible patchwork quilt. “It’s the kind of blanket that feels substantial without trapping heat or feeling stuffy,” she notes. “I feel cocooned without a down comforter, but I’m not smothered when I sleep sans AC in the warmer months. It’s a year-round bedding piece for me, especially since the color palette can lean moodier or more cheerful depending on my sheet selection.”.

According to recent reports, rebecca Udall is a newer name and one worth knowing. Her namesake bedding line is built on romantic, careful details, such as soft-colored decorative embroidery along the sheets. McGregor’s current favorite is this scalloped percale sheet set. “The feel is like a washed percale, crisp but forgiving, and I find that the subtle color on the detailed edge gives the perfect amount of visual interest to my all-white bedscape,” she states. If you want less ornament, try the Georgiana duvet cover, with faint ladderstitch detailing hand-embroidered by artisans in Northern Italy.

Hommey, an Australian brand founded in 2020, first caught on with its boldly striped robes and nightwear. It has since carried those designs into cotton and linen sheets and duvet covers. Across both fabrics, there are more than two dozen colors and prints to choose from. For maximalists who want to try color-blocking, the brand’s bolder colorways are a great place to start.

It has been revealed that baker tested the brown sugar linen duvet cover and found the stonewashed, Oeko-Tex certified flax smoother and more broken-in straight out of the package than the Quince version she already owned (above). “I won’t get ahead of myself and say it feels like pure silk, but I can confirm that it’s soft and breathable almost like an organic cotton duvet after a few washes,” Baker says. She pairs the chocolatey shade with burgundy linen sheets for a moodier bed, though it also works as a neutral with lighter sheets in oatmeal, which pick up the cream trim. The one drawback is that the cover has no interior ties, so the insert can shift around inside.

Recent findings suggest that australian brand Cultiver makes linen sheets and duvets with an easy, beachy look. Its Oeko-Tex certified pieces are an investment, and a worthwhile one. Coverlets are generously sized so they drape loosely, and the envelope-back pillow cases hold their shape without looking stiff. Fletcher has put her set through heavy use and many wash cycles. “Linen is my bedding fabric of choice pretty much 365 days a year, and Cultiver’s high-quality sheet sets do it for me in a way no other brand has. Out of all the sets I’ve tried, this one has stood the test of many washes, my dog digging in them to get cozy at night, and surviving across seasons without feeling worn or threadbare,” she indicates.

Erica Tanov’s bedding is handmade by artisans in Jaipur, in 100% linen with embroidery drawn from traditional Indian textiles. Harrison calls hers “a lifetime set” that “draws more compliments than anything else in my apartment.” The linen is soft and tough: She hauls this sheet set to her neighborhood laundromat, and it survives the communal machines without damage. It’s the first linen set she’s found to be “city-friendly,” as she calls it. She hasn’t tried the quilts or throw blankets yet, though one already tops her birthday wishlist (this one).

It depends mostly on how you like your bed to feel and how reliable your thermostat is. If you like the crisp coolness of hotel sheets, try percale. If you like a soft, organic feel, try linen for a breezy texture, or bamboo sheets for something similar to silk. Cotton sheets (like Supima sets) are often the most durable over time, especially after many, many washes. Your warmest options are generally flannel sets, and your coolest are generally bamboo and percale. For a basic setup, we recommend a full sheet set (flat sheet included, people) plus a duvet insert with a cover. The cover protects the insert and keeps it clean, so you’ll generally only need to wash the insert every six months rather than weekly like your sheets. Harrison likes to go one step further with a bed blanket underneath her duvet and above her sheets for a bit of weight and additional warmth. If a fluffy duvet isn’t your thing, a quilt or coverlet can take its place and add a little more weight.

What to Look for When Buying Bedding.

Industry observers note that start with the fiber content on the label. Search for 100% cotton, linen (the more organic, the better), and steer clear of polyesters or more plastic fibers, as they’re likely to pill more quickly and break apart in the washer and dryer.

Tennis is Aces for Healthy Aging

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (781 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you.
  • It has been revealed that “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” notes sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open.
  • You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if we told you tennis has been shown to boost heart health, balance, strength, mental acuity, and mood plus add nearly 10 years to your life, you might think we also had a bridge to sell you. But it’s true: Research indicates that even recreational tennis can have a seriously impressive impact on your health—now and for years to come.

It has been revealed that “Tennis is a whole-body sport,” notes sports medicine surgeon Alexis Colvin, MD, chief medical officer of the US Open. “It offers cardiovascular benefits, muscle strengthening, flexibility—all the things you need to deal with any physical challenges later in life.”.

You also don’t have to be a star tennis player to reap the longevity benefits, Dr. Colvin adds. In a 2020 study she co-authored, researchers surveyed over 10,000 tennis players, most of them recreational; about 70 percent played just one to three days a week. The players scored higher than the general population on measures such as physical strength, mental and emotional health, and social engagement. “You don't have to be playing at a very high level to get those benefits,” Dr. Colvin says.

And those benefits appear to extend one’s life: When researchers followed 8,577 people for up to 25 years, they found that those who played tennis an average of 103 minutes a week lived 9.7 years longer than their sedentary counterparts. They also lived significantly longer than cyclists (who get an extra 3.7 years), swimmers (3.4 years), and joggers (3.2 years).

Even if you’ve never played tennis before, it’s never too late to start. Keep reading for five reasons to pick up a racket, hit the court, and do your future self a favor.

Tennis involves bursts of high intensity movement—sprinting to the net, running backwards to lob a volley, stopping and then lunging to the opposite side of the court to hit the ball—all of which can do wonders for your cardiovascular health. It boosts heart rate, maximizes your body’s use of oxygen, strengthens heart muscle, improves circulation, and can lower blood pressure and cholesterol levels. As a result, women who play tennis an average two to three hours a week have a 44 percent lower risk of developing cardiovascular disease and a 66 percent lower chance of dying from it.

When you sprint across the court, swing a racquet, or come to a sudden stop, you’re working your leg muscles, core, shoulders, back, and arms—in other words, strengthening nearly every part of the body. A recent study of more than 5,000 women between the ages 63 and 99 found that those who had greater muscle strength lived the longest. And because you’re also supporting your own body weight as you run and land, the sport also helps increase bone density, Dr. Colvin claims. Stronger bones mean a lower risk of fractures and osteoporosis in the future, which is what you need if you want to age well.

Tennis requires coordinated movement and muscle control to maintain fluid footwork and smooth, continuous swings. Your core helps make that possible and is key to good balance. Both core strength and balance can help you avoid falls and fractures as you get older. Another part of balance is visuospatial skill—the ability to recognize environmental cues that help you stay upright. Tennis may help sharpen that, too. In a 2022 study, older tennis players who faced a disruption that could throw them off balance were able to react and steady themselves as well as younger players.

Tennis demands intense focus and decision making. “There’s a lot of active thinking going on,” Dr. Colvin indicates. “You’re making a lot of split-second decisions while you’re playing, plus thinking about the overall strategy of the game. That kind of mental engagement is important as we get older.” According to research, engaging in that kind of quick and strategic thinking while being physically active may be particularly good at promoting neuroplasticity and boosting cognitive function—both of which can stave off the cognitive decline that can come with age.

Studies have found that people who play tennis regularly tend to be less stressed or anxious than people who do lower-intensity exercise. They also report feeling more optimistic, less depressed, and a greater sense of well-being. Like other high-energy sports, tennis may boost mood by prompting the release of brain chemicals such as endorphins, dopamine, and serotonin. It’s also a fun game to play with friends. “The social aspect of tennis is one of its key benefits,” Dr. Colvin claims. Numerous studies show that those kinds of community ties are essential for a long, healthy, happier life. With tennis, that’s built into the game.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police.
  • Industry observers note that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction.
  • It has been revealed that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Tesla driver caught asleep behind the wheel on Ottawa’s Highway 417 during Tuesday’s rush hour now faces a careless driving charge from the Ontario Provincial Police. The photo OPP shared indicates a new-generation Model Y in traffic.

Industry observers note that the charge carries a $490 fine and six demerit points on conviction. It’s at least the fifth time this year Canadian police have gone public with a sleeping Tesla driver, and it’s not a coincidence that it’s happening as “Full Self-Driving” gets better.

It has been revealed that OPP East Region posted about the stop Wednesday morning. Police didn’t name the brand or the driver-assist system, but the message was clear: “even though your vehicle has an autonomous driving feature, drivers are still required to pay due care and attention when behind the wheel.”.

According to OPP, the officer could see the driver’s eyes were closed and hands were off the steering wheel. Instead of lighting up the cruiser, police pulled in close to capture body camera footage first.

Careless driving isn’t a parking ticket in Ontario. The $490 is the set fine, but if the case goes to court, the Highway Traffic Act allows fines up to $2,000, up to six months in jail, and a licence suspension of up to two years.

Ottawa is the latest, but British Columbia has been dealing with this all year:.

Sources indicate that this isn’t new in Canada either. Back in 2020, Alberta RCMP went further and criminally charged a Tesla driver caught sleeping on Autopilot at 150 km/h with dangerous driving.

It has been revealed that the U.S. has the same problem with less enforcement. In September, Colorado State Patrol got a report of a sleeping Tesla driver on I-70 near Georgetown and never found the car. The same month, Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi pressed the DOT after NBC News found 43 videos of drivers apparently asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted in 2026 alone.

And in October, a driver told CHP he was asleep on FSD when his Tesla drove into a closed crash scene and hit a patrol car in Fairfield, California. Two officers were seriously injured.

A few years ago, FSD needed an intervention every few miles, so nobody was napping. You couldn’t.

Now FSD can handle long highway stretches without a takeover, and that’s exactly when supervision breaks down. A human asked to watch a system that’s right 99% of the time stops watching. That’s automation complacency, and it’s one of the most studied problems in aviation and driving research.

Waymo learned this the hard way. In 2013, Google let employees use its highway driver-assist prototype and caught people falling asleep at highway speed. It decided a system that works most of the time but still needs a human to catch its mistakes was the worst of both worlds, and it went straight to driverless.

According to recent reports, tesla went the other way. It sells a Level 2 system called “Full Self-Driving” that’s good enough to lull people to sleep, and it puts the full responsibility on the human who’s now asleep.

Since FSD v12.4, Tesla has relied mainly on the cabin camera above the rearview mirror to make sure the driver is watching the road. But look at what Tesla’s own owner’s manual claims about it: the camera “does not require full visibility of the driver’s eyes in order to monitor attentiveness,” and the system “is still active, for example, if the driver is wearing sunglasses.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, it’s often judging head position, not whether your eyes are open. When it can’t see your hands, it falls back to asking for a bit of torque on the wheel, which a sleeping driver resting a hand on the rim can provide.

Recent findings suggest that the penalties are soft too. Five “strikeouts” suspend FSD for a week, and each strike is forgiven after three and a half days.

And Tesla has been moving in the wrong direction. Musk said in December 2025 that FSD v14.2.1 lets drivers text “depending on context of surrounding traffic.” In May 2026, he said v14.3.3 “nags less too.” When the car does detect drowsiness, Tesla’s alert reads “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” That pushes a tired driver to lean harder on the system instead of pulling over.

Compare that with GM’s Super Cruise, which uses a steering column camera with infrared LEDs to track head and eye position, and only works hands-free on pre-mapped highways.

Recent findings suggest that the Ottawa driver had their eyes closed and their hands off the wheel in rush hour traffic, and the car was still driving when an officer pulled up beside it. Whatever Tesla’s camera was checking from a foot away, it hadn’t stopped the car before a cop in the next lane did.

We’re glad Canadian police are treating this seriously. A $490 fine and six points is a real deterrent, and OPP’s message is the right one: no matter what Tesla calls it, you’re the driver.

Sources indicate that people have been falling asleep at the wheel since driving started; many, if not most, have ended up in tragedy. At least with the self-driving cars, there is a margin of safety, especially for other drivers. These cars should monitor the driver better and pull off the road when it happens.

Recent findings suggest that but police can’t ticket their way out of this. These drivers aren’t edge cases anymore. They’re the predictable result of a system that drives well enough to make people relax, sold under a name that tells them relaxing is fine.

It has been revealed that the fix is on Tesla’s side, and it isn’t complicated. Detect closed eyes, even behind sunglasses, which is what infrared eye-tracking is built for. When a driver doesn’t respond, slow down and pull over immediately instead of escalating warnings for minutes. Stop telling drowsy drivers to “stay focused with FSD.” And make the strike system actually sting.

NHTSA already forced a recall of over 2 million Teslas in December 2023 over weak Autopilot monitoring. Three years later, people are still sleeping through rush hour on FSD.

#64165. The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1118 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

The Power of Kindness in a World Driven by Probability

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.
  • "We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable." —Maria Popova.
  • “I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” —Lady Gaga.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 19, 2026 | Reviewed by Jessica Schrader.

"We place life’s bets by countless calculations of probability, conscious and unconscious, only to discover over and over how short they fall of the wildest reaches of the possible, which always includes but exceeds the probable." —Maria Popova.

“I’ve been searching for ways to heal myself, and I’ve found that kindness is the best way.” —Lady Gaga.

"The question is not: what have I achieved? But rather: who can I be when I am with you? Who can you be when you are with me?" —Nora Bateson.

Sources indicate that we live in a world, at least in our hectic Western-based culture, that is driven by probability. What is probability? How does it taste, smell, or feel? Does it just linger in our complexity, waiting for a never-achieved form? We calculate within probability both with our awareness and unawareness. It penetrates our educational, economic, political, and medical systems. It assumes that we will automatically accept models of certainty. Yet our problems still exist in the domain of probable content.

According to recent reports, probability is all-powerful and designed to make you believe its outcomes are absolute. It waits for our lives to pass through it with definitive rules to fit all. However, it can never seem to guarantee success. It tries to be the basis of caution, yet it can also be the source of the other side of safety. It can, in many instances, be the origin of violence and discrimination.

In a recent development, why? Probability measures the likelihood or chance that a specific event will occur. It survives on unresolved paradoxes of this or that, and that misses the yin/yang, messy/beautifulness of life in all its complexity. It can be funny, as in humor, and puzzling with choices, but when not harnessed, it feels separate and fragmented, avoiding the ecological process of how all patterns connect.

Probability evades the wisdom of understanding how love, altruism, and empathy can breed kindness, which some might consider the regulating homeostasis basis of living systems. Anthropologist Gregory Bateson more than hinted at the misunderstanding of probability’s faults by suggesting that absolute outcomes hide how "Human actions involve play, context, and the probability of disaster or risk within a relationship." Probability makes us too busy to savor what happens between relationships, yet when we do, it can help us step back from absolute outcomes and certainty and find improvisational potential. When we do, with encouragement, this can create all kinds of possibilities. Maria Popova, for instance, mentions in the first stanza of her poem "The Wildest Bet Is the Winning Bet":.

"You wouldn’t have bet on it,the battered rockorbiting a starfrom the discount binof the universe".

Probability dissolves when you zoom outward with your personal lens and widen your perspective, making room for kindness to be born. Probability, in this case, begins to blend with how we share our possessions. It becomes an advocate for tending to others' needs, which gives ultimate meaning to who we are as humans. It becomes the terrain of kindness, the quality or state of being friendly, generous, considerate, and genuinely concerned for the well-being of others. Through kindness, we can choose to blend with the paradoxes inherent in unchecked probability to see an ecological unity in a manner felt by C.S. Lewis, who wrote in Surprised by Joy: "Only when your whole attention and desire are fixed on something else—whether a distant mountain, or the past, or the gods of Asgard—does the 'thrill' arise." That is the prerequisite for kindness.

According to recent reports, using kindness as an ecological framework supports a sense of order in contrast to probability’s search for finite answers. This demand for finitude is what excludes kindness because it depends on producing outcomes. Kindness, however, is driven by understanding the constraints and interdependency of any living system. This is why it is woven into global popular symbolism and metaphors. It is based on maintaining what may be good for humanity rather than accumulating something. It is forming a kinship based on forgiveness, not to condone past pain but to move forward with altruism and empathy. Kindness emerges in what poet Allen Ginsberg poetically called a state that "stretches thru every probability." It is the beginner's mind of temporary emptiness, which can at first seem conceptually liable, mistaken for sheer nothingness, yet is in fact the improvisational potential for possibilities of kindness.

We must recognize this need for kindness, especially in today's struggle to accept diversity. This underscores a profound reminder, particularly useful as we celebrate Thanksgiving, that the Anglo experience in North America began as a big mistake in probability, as Garrison Keillor reminds us: "...we survived only by the kindness of strangers who had every reason to be cruel." In a quote often attributed to Mark Twain, this type of innate empathy is "...the language which the deaf can hear and the blind can see.".

Sources indicate that when the dictates of probability, with seemingly good intentions, succumb to the dark side of fragmented content in our educational systems, isolated profit-driven health mandates, and sociopolitical polarization, the antidote is massive acts of kindness. This releases feel-good neurotransmitters like dopamine, serotonin, and endorphins. It activates the brain's reward center, creating euphoria and emotional warmth. It further reduces stress by soothing the vagus nerve, which recharges and rejuvenates when it feels secure.

It is interesting how unchecked probability is the cloak of "science" that constantly tries to quantify or refute the effects of kindness, when it only needs to observe how it strengthens social bonds like a welcome adhesive. Kindness can increase trust and collaboration, and encourage greater equity in the distribution of wealth, security, and opportunity, allowing for our innate interdependency with each other and nature. Another worthwhile attribute is the resulting togetherness that correlates with lower rates of anxiety and depression. Consider this in contrast to the array of physical ailments that can occur with unchecked probability, and it's a choice worth exploring.

It has been revealed that here are some prompts to help you sustain kindness as an antidote to probability. Use them with someone else or in groups. After each response, follow up with at least five “How did that affect you?” questions and ask how you can make a difference. Then discuss using paraphrasing to provide feedback about what was heard.

A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Indicates

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1074 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” stated study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The upcoming review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

According to recent reports, “Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

Industry observers note that “This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

Sources indicate that “A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein noted.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

According to recent reports, “For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

Sources indicate that sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

But I would also style them with dark denim and a cashmere sweater. The side zipper makes getting dressed a little less of a production in the morning. Recent findings suggest that now, these are the most expensive boots on this list, but because they’re made in Italy using Blake-stitched construction, a technique that stitches the upper directly to the sole for a slimmer, more flexible profile than you’d typically get with bulkier boot construction. The latest Volkswagen ID. Tiguan will be available with two battery packs and three performance levels:.

‘One-in-a-million’ yellow fish found in New York

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (465 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that we’ll call him mellow yellow.
  • Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia.
  • According to recent reports, the team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’ll call him mellow yellow. An “exceptionally rare” yellow-colored burbot (Lota lota) was recently caught by a team of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) biologists in Oswego Harbor on Lake Ontario in Upstate Fresh York.

Burbots are long fish that weigh about three to five pounds on average, and live in cold rivers and lakes of North America, Europe, and Asia. To the naked eye, they appear scaleless, but are actually covered with tiny, almost microscopic scales. What they eat depends on their size. Smaller burbots will eat zooplankton, while bigger burbots prefer to snack on other fish.

According to recent reports, the team caught the brightly colored fish during a routine aquatic invasive species survey. It gets its unique color from a rare genetic condition called xanthochromism. A genetic mutation suppresses the normal pigmentation, it produces a yellow-orange appearance instead of the burbot’s usual grey, olive, or tan coloring. In wild fish, xanthochromism is less common than albinism or melanism, making this fish an “especially unusual capture.”.

Recent findings suggest that the burbot is a native species in the Great Lakes, but the USFWS team says the discovery highlights the effectiveness of the Service’s Aquatic Invasive Species Early Detection and Monitoring Program. The program uses a multi-gear fish-surveillance strategy to detect certain non-native species in the harbors, rivers, and embayments of the Great Lakes. Early detection of a watchlist species gives fisheries managers the best opportunity to implement prevention and removal measures if invasive species are detected. Since invasive species are often rare when they first enter fresh waters, the program uses electrofishing, fyke-netting, gill-netting, and environmental DNA (eDNA) analysis to increase the chances that scientists detect an invasive species.

“The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low, and the species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor,” the USFWS wrote in a statement. “It represents the first documented detection of a burbot during a fisheries survey in Oswego Harbor, although a few angler catches have been reported.”.

Industry observers note that the United States Geological Survey (USGS) fisheries biologists, who examined the fish and are familiar with the species, also observed that it was very thin and appeared to be in poor health. It was later sent to the Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine for a health analysis due to the “unexplained factors contributing to the continued suppression of its population”.

“The discovery could turn out to be lucky for the burbot too; this exceptionally rare fish may provide valuable insight into the health of the species’ populations throughout the basin that can inform management actions,” the USFWS concluded.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the big screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic.
  • After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, while most people race to the hospital to give birth, Ginger Rogers’s mother, Lela, insisted that her baby girl’s first breaths be taken in their Missouri home. “The little four-room house at 100 Moore Street was the perfect choice” for the future icon’s July 1911 welcome to the world, Rogers concluded in her 1991 memoir, Ginger: My Story. The star would go on to live with her extended family in Kansas City at 3306 Bellefountain Street; with her stepfather in Fort Worth at 1510 Cooper Street; and once she became a Hollywood sensation, a sprawling Beverly Hills estate. That joy and sense of peace she found in her childhood residence became a defining feature of her California pad. “It was a fun house, a happy house,” Rogers told Architectural Digest in 1994. “I was never angry when I didn’t have to work, because I liked to stay home so much.”.

Decades after her death in 1995, Rogers is poised to return to the big screen by way of Sabrina Carpenter, who’s set to portray the late actor in the forthcoming, yet-to-be-titled Fred Astaire biopic. Tom Holland will star as Astaire. Read on for a glimpse inside the Oscar winner’s off-set life in the places she cherished most.

Rogers on the diving board in 1938.

After Rogers separated from her second husband, actor Lew Ayres, in 1936, she and her mother moved in together. “I asked Mother if she would like me to build her a house, and if she did, could I live in it with her,” Rogers wrote in her memoir. “The next day she scoured the area for a suitable place to build. She found a wonderful lot high in Beverly Hills on 2.75 acres on Gilcrest Drive in Coldwater Canyon. It had a view that didn’t stop; when the fog burned off late every afternoon, it was possible to see Catalina.” Rogers is pictured at the stunning estate in this 1938 photo.

The actor with her home ice cream fountain.

Recent findings suggest that the Swing Time star added many personal touches to the home, one of which was an elaborate soda fountain. In this 1940 photo, she’s shown whipping up a sweet treat. In her memoir, Rogers recalled all the amenities she installed. “The building took over a year because of labor strikes and material shortages,” she wrote. “When the house was finished, it proved to have been worth waiting for. It had everything I wanted or needed in a house: swimming pool, tennis court, projection room, and my very own soda fountain. Who could ask for anything more?”.

Rogers opened her home tennis court to championship hopefuls so they could get practice matches in.

Rogers was an avid tennis player. Though she’s pictured here in 1950 at her Malibu beach house, the actor also had a home court installed at Gilcrest Drive. “On the way to the pool and tennis court were eight sculptured bay leaf trees. Next to the blue-tiled pool was my tennis court. This was my pride and joy,” she wrote in Ginger: My Story. With the knowledge that Rogers had the only en-tout-cas court in the area, the Tennis Association “begged” her to invite young hopefuls for some practice before they went on to championship matches at Forest Hills, New York. “I was delighted to open my court to competitors like Pancho Gonzales, Gussie Moran; and, later, Billie Jean King, Jennifer Hood, and Alice Marble slammed a few over the net too,” Rogers remarked.

Rogers was known for hosting her Hollywood star friends at home in Beverly Hills.

The Top Hat actor’s Beverly Hills abode was also a hot party spot for Rogers’s A-list friends. “My home was made for entertaining and I gave party after party,” she wrote in her memoir. “Most of them were informal. I’d serve spaghetti and we’d play some night tennis. Alcohol was never served, just cold drinks. One, a mixture of finely crushed ice, 7-Up, and concentrated orange juice, was a real favorite with the tennis crowd.”.

The star had a close relationship with her mother, Lela.

Rogers loved living with her mother, with whom she’s pictured in the circa 1940s portrait on the piano in this 1954 image. The triple threat pushed back against the term “stage mother” in Architectural Digest; she considered her mom to be “my guide and my professor… she was my encyclopedia. She knew what route to take: She helped Lucille Ball along hers too, you know. It would have been hard to have a career without her.” About their Beverly Hills pad, she added, “we both liked the look of a French farmhouse. And I wanted certain specific things: a helpful bath, a tennis court, and my own projection room, where we had eight or ten director’s chairs, so that friends could come over to watch movies.”.

Rogers with a furry friend at home in the 1950s.

According to recent reports, the home featured a main house with bedrooms for Rogers and her mom, as well as a guesthouse for visitors. “The house was very bright,” she told Architectural Digest. “I don’t like dark things; even in my clothing, I prefer to be light and colorful—Springtime for Henry has always been my motto,” she explained, referencing the 1934 comedy. In her memoir, Rogers added, “The style was an American farmhouse with Dutch doors opening to cool breezes. The large bay window in the corner of the living room had a view of Beverly Hills and a bit of Los Angeles. Off the living room was a patio for barbecuing on a flagstone area under a beautiful Australian pepper tree. It was a wonderful place to entertain on crisp California nights.”.

Rogers’s home also included a solarium, and bedrooms with scenic views. “On a lower level was an outside entrance to the playroom,” the actor noted in her memoir. “This room had big windows and comfortable cushions as did the solarium in the hallway to the patio. I read many a book, with apple in hand, buried in those downy cushions.” About her bedrooms, she added, “There were two bedrooms leading from the solarium, one for Lelee [her mother] with a four-posted bed and one for me. My room looked out on the view of Beverly Hills, and I had a beautiful hand-carved mantel for my fireplace.”.

Rogers at work on an oil painting.

According to recent reports, in addition to the stage talents for which she became a star, Rogers was also a painter. Her guesthouse also doubled as a studio. “My studio, which could double as a guesthouse, held all the paraphernalia of my hobbies: painting materials, canvases, paintbrushes, turpentine, pencils, and so on,” she wrote in her memoir. “Whenever there was a lull on set, I’d take out my pencil and sketch,” Rogers added. “I had been drawing for a long time and it seemed to come naturally to me. I found it challenging and relaxing. I never studied drawing or painting, I just did it.”.

In her memoir, Rogers recalled a time when she brought her paintings out for a gallery show. “When I’m not working or traveling, my main source of relaxation comes from my painting,” she wrote. “Gallery owners have wanted to have a one-person show of my work, but I never had the time to organize my paintings. Well, now was the time. Gregg Juarez, a gallery owner and friend of mine, arranged for a show and sale at his gallery in Palm Desert. As we were hanging the paintings for display, I realized these were my children—I couldn’t sell them! Gregg told me I had to sell a few so the customers wouldn’t get mad. I managed to put a few up for sale, but couldn’t part with the rest. So now they are joyously hung in my home for all to see.”.

Rogers was 83 years old when she died in 1995 at home in California.

Rogers remained at her home on Gilcrest Drive until 1970, when her mom urged her to sell while she was away working in Europe. “I had been renting it out more than living in it lately, and Mother thought it was financially sound to put it on the market,” the actor wrote in her memoir. “Besides, she said it needed a newly introduced roof! She handled all the details of the sale…. This was one time I’m not sure Mother knew best. I adored that house on Gilcrest Drive and have regretted selling it ever since.” Rogers died decades later, on April 25, 1995, at her home in Rancho Mirage, per the Los Angeles Times.

Breaking: 9-foot-tall Game Boy Color plays all the classics

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1450 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci
