Muscle Size vs. Strength: Which Matters More for Living Longer? Experts Explain

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body.
  • Sources indicate that resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength.
  • In a recent development, on the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when it comes to aging well, you've probably heard that building muscle is one of the best things you can do for your body. And it's true: Maintaining muscle mass is essential for staying healthy, mobile, and independent as you get older. But here's something you might not realize: Having more muscle doesn't necessarily mean you're stronger. And when it comes to living as long (and as well!) as possible, that distinction matters.

Sources indicate that resistance training, which is often used as an umbrella term, can have different goals, including building muscle size and increasing maximal strength. Training for muscle growth, known as hypertrophy training, focuses on increasing the size of your muscles, states Vonda Wright, MD, an orthopedic surgeon who researches longevity and muscle health.

In a recent development, on the other hand, training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force your muscles can produce. It’s often measured by how much weight you can lift in a particular exercise, Dr. Wright explains. Although larger muscles have the potential to produce more force, muscle size alone doesn’t determine strength. “That’s why someone who is smaller can sometimes be stronger than someone with visibly larger muscles,” she adds.

Meet the experts: Vonda Wright, MD, is an orthopedic surgeon and author of Unbreakable. Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, is an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute in Atlanta. Stuart Phillips, PhD, is a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Ben Walker, CPT, is a personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland.

It has been revealed that still, both adaptations play an vital role in healthy aging—especially since muscle mass and strength naturally decline with age. Building muscle supports your joints and bones, helps regulate metabolic health, and gives you the strength and physical capacity to keep moving and stay active, states Mark Kovacs, PhD, CSCS, an exercise physiologist, longevity and human performance specialist, and founder of the Kovacs Institute. Strength, meanwhile, allows you to put that muscle to work, whether you’re carrying groceries, climbing stairs, or getting up from the floor, he explains.

It has been revealed that it’s imperative to build both strength and muscle for a long, healthy life. But if your goal is to stay active and independent well into your later years, one may be worth prioritizing over the other.

According to recent reports, resistance training can help you build muscle and become stronger, but these are distinct goals that emphasize different outcomes. Training for muscle growth focuses on increasing muscle size, while training for maximal strength focuses on improving how much force you can produce, says Kovacs. The two goals overlap, and people typically gain both muscle and strength through resistance training. But you can formulate your workouts to emphasize one outcome over the other, he adds.

It has been revealed that for instance, if your goal is maximal strength, the weight you lift matters more. So, training for strength means practicing movements with loads that feel heavy to you, says Stuart Phillips, PhD, a muscle researcher and professor of kinesiology at McMaster University. Strength gains depend not only on muscle size, but also on how effectively your nervous system activates your muscles and how efficiently you perform the movement. “Lighter weights can still make you stronger, but taking them to failure doesn’t automatically make them equivalent to heavier training for maximizing strength,” Phillips explains. For this goal, he recommends 2 to 3 sets of roughly 4 to 8 reps with a challenging weight, stopping before your technique breaks down.

In terms of muscle growth, both lighter and heavier weights can build muscle—what matters is that your body is sufficiently challenged. Of course, lighter weights will require more repetitions to grow muscle, Phillips notes. (In fact, his research reveals that performing roughly 20 to 25 repetitions with light weights produced similar muscle growth to sets of 8 to 12 repetitions with heavier weights when both were taken to failure.).

In a recent development, as a rule of thumb, Phillips recommends choosing a weight that makes the last few reps feel challenging while leaving about two good reps in reserve. (If you finish 25 reps and feel like you could easily do five more, the weight is probably too light to provide enough of a stimulus to spark growth.) One way to gauge this is with the resistance-training rating of perceived exertion (RPE) scale, which measures how hard a set feels based on how many more reps you think you could complete with good form, he explains. The scale runs from 1 to 10: An RPE of eight means you could squeeze out about two more reps, a 9 means you have one left, and a 10 means you’ve reached failure and can’t complete another rep.

Sources indicate that the number of sets you perform matters for building muscle, too. Doing one challenging set per exercise consistently over time can grow muscle, Phillips says, but research suggests that performing multiple sets generally leads to greater muscle growth.

Strength, which is the maximum force you can produce in a particular task, directly influences how well you can move through everyday life. “Strong muscles support our skeleton, protect our joints, improve metabolic health, and allow us to continue doing the things we love at 50, 70, and 90,” states Dr. Wright. Strength helps us with getting up off the floor, carrying our own suitcase, climbing a mountain, playing with grandchildren, and living independently long-term.

Consider something as simple as getting out of a chair. When you’re younger and stronger, Kovacs claims that movement may require only a small percentage of your maximum strength. As you lose strength with age, though, that same movement requires more of what you have available. If you aren’t regularly training it, everyday activities can become increasingly difficult, he explains. But when you continue to build strength as you age, you have more to pull from, making those activities easier.

Industry observers note that additionally, research draws a direct connection between strength and a longer life: A 2026 study in JAMA Network Open looked at the association between muscular strength and mortality. Over 5,000 women ages 63 to 99 underwent testing for grip strength, chair stand performance, and a timed walk test. Participants also mailed health update questionnaires annually between 2012 and 2014 until 2023. They found that higher muscle strength was associated with lower mortality.

Industry observers note that strength training is also associated with cardiometabolic benefits, endurance performance, and bone density—which are all vital for living long and well. In fact, a small 2022 study in Sensors had 29 postmenopausal women with osteopenia or osteoporosis (when you have lower bone mineral density than normal) either do strength training exercises with heavy and moderately heavy weights, or no exercise at all, for six months. The group that strength trained had higher bone mineral density at the end of the trial period.

Muscle is one of your body’s best forms of insurance for getting older. Everyday activities depend on having enough muscle (as well as strength) to do them independently. “Muscle supports our joints and loads our bones, helping stimulate the bone-building process, but it’s also essential to mobility and functional strength," Dr. Wright explains. “If we want to continue getting ourselves off the ground, climbing stairs, carrying things, traveling, playing sports, and living independently, we need muscle to do it.”.

Research also concludes that less muscle mass is associated with a higher risk of mortality. A 2023 review in PLOS One observed 16 studies with over 81,000 participants and looked at the connection between their body composition and when they died. The review concluded that a low skeletal muscle mass index was significantly associated with an increased risk of all-cause mortality.

According to recent reports, additionally, having muscle mass can improve your metabolic health. A 2025 study in Nutrition & Metabolism had older participants with type 2 diabetes either build muscle through resistance training alone, resistance training and eating a whey protein supplement, or doing neither of the two, for 12 weeks. Those who completed the muscle-building interventions significantly improved their blood glucose control and insulin resistance.

Recent findings suggest that plus, lower muscle mass is linked to poor balance and a higher risk of falls. So, maintaining muscle helps protect your mobility and independence as you age, Dr. Wright adds. A 2020 study in Menopause Review had 122 women over 60 do physical performance tests (gait speed test, grip strength, and a timed up and go). Their body composition was measured, and they filled out a survey of how often they fell in the past year. Less muscle was associated with a higher risk of falls.

A well-rounded workout plan should naturally progress both muscular size and strength. After all, they address different pieces of the same puzzle and one form of training can help you make progress in the other. As you build muscle, you generally increase the amount of tissue available to produce force, says Ben Walker, CPT, a certified personal trainer and founder of Anywhere Fitness in Dublin, Ireland. And as you train for strength, your brain and nervous system become better at coordinating and activating those muscles, he explains.

In a recent development, if you’re looking for a plan that’ll help you build both strength and muscle, check out our Women’s Health+ exclusive workout aims. Each one comes with four weeks of expert-programmed workouts, science-backed nutrition advice, and evidence-based recovery methods.

It has been revealed that remember, longevity isn’t about simply adding years to your life. It’s about extending your healthspan, or the number of years you remain healthy, mobile, and strong. “The goal is to bring our healthspan as close to our lifespan as possible, and for me, that means building a body that can carry you through the life you want to live,” claims Dr. Wright. That way, you’ll be ready to throw grandkids around at 60, deadlift hundreds of pounds at 70, and lift your own suitcase on vacation with your family in your 80s and beyond.

#64080. Why "Face-to-Face Only" Might Be Costing You Good Therapy

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1434 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Psychologytoday ↗ Open Full Page

Why "Face-to-Face Only" Might Be Costing You Good Therapy

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1434 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.
  • I’ve been noticing a trend, a shift, across psychology and therapy platforms.
  • Prior to COVID, I swore I would never do telehealth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Tyler Woods.

I’ve been noticing a trend, a shift, across psychology and therapy platforms. It’s the “only face-to-face” request. “In person only,” “No telehealth,” from referral requests to consumers, I see it everywhere.

Look, I get it. I truly get it. Prior to COVID, I swore I would never do telehealth. Only in rare cases, where it was the only way someone would get support, would I even consider it.

In a recent development, so, understandably, the start of COVID was not an easy transition for me. Lockdowns meant that those rare cases where I would consider it now applied to everyone, and people needed support more than ever. So, like many of my colleagues, I did the training, dived deep on what was possible, and did the best I could. And what I found were... results. It was not the terrible outcome I had anticipated, but more than that, it was not just something to hold the fort until I could get back to ‘real therapy’. It worked. So, post-COVID, I started doing more, until now, full disclaimer: I run a telehealth-only practice, so it’s fair to say I may hold some bias in this space.

Recent findings suggest that I also get why the pendulum has swung. Post-COVID, we're living in a world where a lot of us are lacking face-to-face connections. We spent years on screens, we worked on screens, we saw our families on screens, our kids went to school on screens, we threw our birthday parties on, yup, screens. So it makes sense that we've come out the other side and decided, maybe rightly so, that online interactions just aren't as good. Here’s this thing, I back this, we absolutely do need face-to-face interactions. But this is where we get stuck in black-and-white thinking. Online bad; in-person good. Rather than leveraging screen time to buy us more face-to-face in the spaces that matter most.

But you folks know me, let’s check what the evidence actually indicates about it all.

Sources indicate that telehealth therapy has actually been shown to be as effective as face-to-face therapy. A 2021 meta-analysis comparing live video therapy with in-person therapy found that therapy is no less effective when it's delivered by video, with the strongest results for CBT for depression and anxiety. The authors concluded that video therapy isn't just the convenient choice, it's one now backed by evidence. A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials in children, adolescents and their parents found the same thing. Video therapy was as effective as in-person treatment, both straight after treatment and at follow-up.

This was seen in couples' work too. A study of over 1,100 married clients in couple therapy found teletherapy was as effective as in-person therapy for outcomes including relationship satisfaction, sexual satisfaction and the therapeutic alliance.

Sources indicate that the big worry I hear, from clinicians especially, is about the therapeutic relationship. Can you really connect through a screen? It's a fair question, and the honest answer from what I have found is that the alliance holds up well. A review of studies on this found a good working alliance and good outcomes across all of them, and outcomes that were equivalent to face-to-face. Now, the alliance scores sat a touch lower on average, and the research isn't conclusive yet that they're fully equal. But the outcomes held up.

This is the major bit I think we're missing. If what we're craving is more in-person connection, telehealth might actually be part of how we get it. It potentially allows us more time to engage in person in the situations that are more meaningful.

We can fit our therapy around our work and our lives, and save that key face-to-face time for family, friends, and community. The hour you'd have spent driving across town, finding parking, sitting in a waiting room and driving home again? That could be dinner with your kids. A walk with a friend. Actually turning up to the thing you keep saying you'll go to. This is no way going to be the case for everyone, but again, if we get stuck in that black-and-white thinking that one is superior to the other, then those who would actually benefit end up missing out.

The other thing to consider, particularly when we look at sex therapy, is that there's some emerging evidence it might actually be easier for us to talk about things like sex, and those topics that feel vulnerable and exposing, when we have this perceived barrier or distance between us.

In a recent development, psychologist John Suler described this back in 2004 as the online disinhibition effect: some people self-disclose more often, or more intensely, online than they would in person. We usually talk about the toxic side of that, the trolls and the pile-ons. But Suler also described the flip side, where people share more openly and ask for help more freely.

Sources indicate that we see a version of this in sexual health research, too. Studies comparing computer-based questionnaires with face-to-face interviews consistently find people report more sensitive sexual behaviours when there's a screen rather than a person in front of them. In one survey from the Cleveland Clinic, 44% of men said they'd prefer to talk to their doctor about sexual health problems online or by phone because they were too embarrassed to do it face-to-face.

Industry observers note that back to COVID, when sexologists in Portugal were surveyed about moving their work online during lockdown, many reported that their clients felt less exposed, with fewer psychological and emotional barriers to get past. So being at home could ease some of the tension about opening up and remove some of the barriers when it comes to getting help for sexual issues. Some also stated it made it easier for clients to talk about gender and sexual orientation, with less stigma. That tracks with what I see in my day-to-day too.

Absolute disclaimer: None of this means telehealth is right for everyone, or every time. Some people don't have a private space at home. Some couples find it hard to get uninterrupted time together without kids. Some people need the ritual of leaving the house and going somewhere. And yes, sometimes that disinhibition means people share a lot, rapidly, and, as therapists, we need to pace that with care.

Sources indicate that but "face-to-face only" as a blanket rule? That's the black-and-white thinking I’m not so sure about. It might be ruling out a therapist who's exactly right for you. It might be ruling out the very format that would make it easier to say the hard thing. Like most things when it comes to psychology, I suggest we move into a space of curiosity rather than good/bad and make a choice that fits best for individual needs.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States.
  • Industry observers note that the hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use.
  • It has been revealed that while both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Three years ago, Mercedes-Benz rolled out the first Level 3 autonomy system offered in the United States. That system is no longer available in the latest revision to the S-Class, with CTO Jörg Burzer calling it “early.” The brand still has advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) ambitions, though, and two newly introduced major products are arriving for a few customers starting next year. Mercedes-Benz has announced aims to launch both hands-free highway driving and hands-on point-to-point navigation in 2027, part of a continuing partnership with (scandal-laden) semiconductor superpower Nvidia. The latter system is subscription-only, although pricing for that subscription has yet to be revealed.

Industry observers note that the hands-free system is limited to “eligible roads,” effectively making it a specialized feature for freeway use. It works up to 85 miles per hour, allowing a driver to take their hands off all inputs while the system handles highway driving and decision-making under the driver’s active supervision. Point-to-point navigation, on the other hand, is a hands-on system with more freedom. Like Tesla or Rivian’s similar offerings, it is intended to handle most of the workload of city driving and react in real time to the peculiarities of that task.

It has been revealed that while both systems reach closer to true autonomous driving, their designation as SAE Level 2 systems mean that they are still nowhere near complete autonomy. That label means that they are meant to be seen as driver assistance systems only, leaving the person in the driver’s seat ultimately responsible for intervening before a problem occurs. The same is true of every autonomous solution currently on offer, including systems marketed as “Full Self-Driving” by Tesla.

Sources indicate that some California residents will receive the opportunity to try both systems starting in December; hands-free driving is expected to reach eligible cars more broadly in spring of 2027, while point-to-point navigation is made available nationwide at some point during the next year. Subscription pricing has not yet been announced, but brand representatives have suggested to Road & Track that it will be “competitive” with similar offerings from other automakers.

Mercedes allowed outlets, including Road & Track, to test both systems in San Francisco ahead of the news. You can read more about how the latest ADAS offerings fared here.

The third-generation Tang joins the Great Tang, or Da Tang, as it’s called in China in BYD’s expanding flagship SUV lineup.

We knew it was coming soon after the latest model appeared in a regulatory filing in China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) last month.

The two lower-priced variants are both RWD, offering a CLTC range of up to 850 km (528 miles), while the top-spec dual-motor AWD version has up to 770 km (478 miles).

All versions use BYD’s second-generation Blade Batteries and Flash Charging tech, enabling the battery to be charged from 10% to 80% in five minutes, or nine minutes to go from 10% to 97%.

Unlike its predessor, which offered five and six-seat configurations, the third-gen Tang will only be offered as a five-seater.

The five-seat setup opens up interior space for passengers and the third-gen Tang has the largest front trunk (frunk) in its class at 205L, BYD said.

Like many of its fresh flagship vehicles, the third-gen Tang is equipped with BYD’s latest tech, including its God’s Eye B driver-assistance system and Disus-A dual-chamber intelligent air suspension body control system.

Other added features include a 22-speaker Dynaudio sound system, intelligent electric all‑wheel drive, a high-speed tire blowout stability system, and its iTAC intelligent torque control system.

Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty division mentioned third-gen Tang vehicles have arrived at dealerships nationwide.

Since its official launch, the larger Great Tang (Da Tang) has sold more than 10,000 units for four straight months now.

Starting at just 269,900 yuan ($40,000), the Flagship EV version uses a bigger (130.15 kWh) battery, offering a CLTC range of up to 590 miles (950 km).

One little bear cub in Southeastern Alaska’s Tongass National Forest is a true model of bravery. The park’s rangers have awarded the unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) cub with the 2026 Courageous Cub award for persevering when he got himself in a little pickle this summer. The cub belongs to a forgetful mother bear named Dory, who had two cubs this season.

Recent findings suggest that “This little cub of Dory’s went on a substantial adventure. He got lost, ran down the trail a half mile and approached visitors as if to ask, ‘Are you my mommy?’ Then got scared and ran off in the wrong direction,” the Tongass rangers write. “Hours later he came running back up the trail sniffing out where mama was.”.

Sources indicate that black bears like this family have a very keen sense of smell. It is debated just how far away they can smell, but it is at least two miles and could be up to 20. Fortunately, the cub was able to use some of that sniffing power to find both Dory and his other sibling.

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are at the moment awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

In a recent development, tongass is the largest national forest in the United States. It covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau, and includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. This makes the creek a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, at least 39 bears feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their chunky counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

Sources indicate that the new entry-level EV is “the last piece of the puzzle,” Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer noted last March after unveiling the ID. EVERY1 concept car.

Volkswagen said the production version will launch in 2027 with a starting price of around €20,000 ($22,000).

Recent findings suggest that the latest model will sit below the ID. Polo in Volkswagen’s Electric Urban Car Family, a lineup of compact, affordable electric cars.

Volkswagen’s current entry-level EV lineup includes the ID. Polo, ID. Cross, the Cupra Raval, and Skoda Epiq, all based on its new MEB+ platform.

According to recent reports, after launching the lower-priced standard versions of the ID. Polo and ID. Cross recently, starting at €24,995 and €27,995, respectively, Volkswagen is preparing to launch an even smaller, more affordable EV next year.

A recent trademark filing with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) and the German DPMA may have just revealed the name of VW’s upcoming €20,000 EV.

In a recent development, volkswagen filed a trademark application for the name ID. UP on October 22, 2026, with the EUIPO and DPMA, suggesting this will be the name of the upcoming electric car in 2027.

Industry observers note that the trademark follows previous reports that VW planned to revive the former Up! name as part of its shift away from its previous numerical naming scheme (ID.3, ID.4, ID.5, etc.).

According to recent reports, volkswagen has kept most details a secret thus far. Like the ID. Polo, the first to go on sale with an established VW nameplate, the ID. UP is expected to use the same 37 kWh LFP battery to reduce costs.

Industry observers note that the VW ID. Polo with the 37 kWh battery offers a WLTP range of up to 334 km (207 miles), so the smaller ID. UP will likely provide around the same, if not slightly more.

Recent findings suggest that the production version of the ID. EVERY1, expected to arrive as the ID. UP, will be one of nine new models VW prepares to launch by 2027.

The VW Group’s upcoming Electric Urban Car Family is off to a strong start, securing nearly 150,000 orders after series production began in June.

All models within the family are built on the MEB+ platform with a FWD powertrain, and share more than 80% of the components and tech.

In a recent development, volkswagen said the production version of the ID. EVERY1 will be among the first vehicles based on its zonal, software-defined vehicle (SDV) architecture, which it is developing through its joint venture with Rivian.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition.
  • Sources indicate that “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it took a few hours longer than expected, but the SS United States now rests at the bottom of the Gulf of Mexico. The nearly 1,000-foot-long ocean liner sank off the coast of Pensacola, Florida, to a depth of about 190 feet on November 11, where it is now officially the world’s largest artificial reef. In the years ahead, biologists and conservationists will monitor the vessel’s remains as numerous marine species slowly convert the ship into their own home.

Sources indicate that ahead of the next phase in the United States’ recycled life, divers from the RV Explorer swam to document the vessel’s location and post-scuttling condition. On November 13, the team released a brief video of their successful excursion. Interestingly, the footage shows the ship is resting upright on the ocean floor despite initially sinking on its side.

Sources indicate that “It was just epic,” diver Rustin Cassway told a local Philadelphia news outlet. “It was very cleaned up. I mean, you could see people really took their time to clean it really nicely.”.

Recent findings suggest that the project marks the first time ecologists will be able to monitor a shipwreck’s transformation in real-time. Researchers now plan to conduct annual visits to the SS United States to chart not only the artificial reef’s progress, but how the ship’s materials may affect the surrounding ocean conditions.

In its heyday, the SS United States was the world’s fastest ocean liner. Larger than the RMS Titanic, she was the most powerful, advanced, and modern passenger liner when she first took to the ocean in 1952. In addition to the 1,700 passengers, 7,935 quarts of ice cream and 500 pounds of caviar were also on board. During that maiden voyage (July 3-7, 1952), she broke the transatlantic speed record held by the RMS Queen Mary by over 10 hours. The United States made the crossing from the United Kingdom to New York in three days, 10 hours, and 40 minutes at an average speed of 40.96 mph.

According to recent reports, she was designed by naval architect William Francis Gibbs (August 24, 1886 – September 6, 1967), and was built to be converted into a troopship if the United States Navy needed during a time of war. But she never was called into military service. Instead, the United States transported immigrants and celebrities, including future President and First Lady John and Jacqueline Kennedy, actors Grace Kelly, Gary Cooper, and Marilyn Monroe, artist Salvador Dali, and musicians Duke Ellington and Irving Berlin. Walt Disney even filmed parts of the 1962 comedy Bon Voyage aboard the ship.

An engineering marvel, some of the key design features were in the rudder, radar mast, and propellers.

In a recent development, the rudder was designed for good maneuverability at high speeds. The Titanic’s relatively small rudder was one factor behind the ship’s collision with an iceberg and tragic sinking in 1912.

Industry observers note that the SS United States had the latest radar equipment, which allowed the crew to see the locations of  other ships and objects in the ocean despite the weather. It was among the first ocean liners to use radar, which was located at one of the highest points on the ship, so in addition to her radar “eyes,” a lookout could be stationed there to warn the captain of any danger in the ship’s path.

According to recent reports, considered a top-secret design, the ship had four propellers—two with four blades and two with five. According to the SS United States Conservancy, this configuration was tested and selected for its superior hydrodynamic performance. The propeller design was overseen by a pioneering Gibbs & Cox engineer named Elaine Kaplan.

In a recent development, ocean liners became a less attractive option once air travel became quicker and less expensive. The SS United States ceased operations in 1969, and stayed in drydock in several cities before becoming the world’s largest artificial reef.

#64073. These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2191 w)

These Fragrances Double As Skincare Products

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2191 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom.
  • I was transfixed by the ritual of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

I REMEMBER being about 10 years old and spending hours in my grandmother’s product-strewn bathroom. In the middle of her pink-tiled bathroom was a small alcove with a skirted makeup table. Perched on top were probably a dozen, maybe more, intricately detailed glass perfume bottles and coordinating scented powders. The fragranced dusting powders were applied with oversized, almost-feathery puffs to absorb oil from the skin and leave it smelling fresh and clean, while the perfume itself acted like a topper, locking in the coordinating scent.

I was transfixed by the ritual of it. Scent has always been an emotional lure of sorts. Whether it transports you back in time or conjures up a memory, the connections that fragrances evoke are personal and emotional. All that unfolds once a fragrance makes contact with the skin. As the notes dance and bloom, the scent really takes hold. But what if the skin-scent connection went one step further? Could a fragrance improve the tone, texture, quality, and health of our skin?

It’s no longer a theoretical—it’s reality.

Dual-purpose beauty products once used to be a one-off. Nowadays, it’s expected that a product will tackle two challenges at once. “We’ve already seen growing interest in functional fragrances, scents formulated with sensitive skin in mind, and alternative fragrance formats like hair mists and body oils, so it’s not surprising to see brands exploring ways to incorporate skincare ingredients into traditional fragrance formats,” notes Darryl Do, a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. The idea of perfume that offers skincare benefits is fitting, and, quite honestly, maybe even a little late to the game. “It feels relevant as consumers become more conscious of the ingredients in their beauty products and what they intend to deliver.”.

In a recent development, meet the experts: Darryl Do is a senior perfumer and fragrance expert at Delbia Do Fragrance & Flavors. Jenna Queller, MD, is a dermatologist and founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton. Charlene Valledor is a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. Farah K. Ahmed is president and CEO of the fragrance creators association (FCA).

As skincare and scent merges into a brand-new category, some are wondering what took so long. “Scent has long been part of wellness rituals,” states Farah K. Ahmed, President & CEO Fragrance Creators Association (FCA). “What’s different today is that we have science showing that functional fragrances actually work.” We spoke with scent experts and a cosmetic chemist for the backstory on the trend and how to make the most of fragrances infused with skincare so that your skin can reap the benefits.

According to recent reports, skin and scent have a long-standing connection. “In the fragrance industry, the term “skin scent” describes fragrances that are close to the natural scent the skin has and complement it rather than overpowering it,” states Do. But how a scent wears on the skin varies. Skin chemistry has a lot to do with how fragrance molecules develop on the skin and mix with your natural scent.

According to recent reports, it’s a matter of body chemistry, which includes pH, how much natural oil is produced by your skin, moisture and perspiration levels, and natural body odor, explains Charlene Valledor, a cosmetic chemist and the co-founder and president of SOS Beauty. “All of that impacts how fragrances smell on the skin and how long it lasts,” she states. That’s why the very same perfume can smell wildly different from one person to the next. Someone with a skin pH of 5.75, more sebum, or who eats a spicy diet, for example, will provide a different environment than someone with a skin pH of 4.75, drier skin, and eats virtually no spicy foods.

But it doesn’t stop there: What you apply to your skin before perfume also influences how a fragrance takes hold. By the time most people finish their morning routine, they’ve already created a fragrance profile and applying perfume introduces another fragrance on top of that existing baseline, Do notes.

Unfortunately, your skin doesn’t always play nicely with certain scents. The ingredients in the bottle themselves, which includes everything from the concentration of alcohol in a scent to the presence of essential oils can cause itching, redness, and general irritation. “Fragrance can directly disrupt skin’s protective barrier or trigger an outright allergic reaction,” explains board-certified dermatologist Jenna Queller, MD, founder of DermWorks in Boca Raton, FL. “Irritation can happen to anyone, particularly when the skin is already dry or compromised. An allergy is different: the immune system has become sensitized to a specific ingredient.”.

It has been revealed that unbeknownst to many, fragrance exposure is cumulative, meaning the more you use a perfume or scented product, the more your skin is exposed to the ingredients. Dr. Queller says that while certain compounds like cinnamal, eugenol, isoeugenol, and geraniol are well-known contact allergens and can damage or irritate the outer layer of skin and weaken the protective barrier, others, such as limonene and linalool, which are commonly found in citrus, floral, and herbal fragrances, can become more allergenic after exposure to air. “Concentration matters because higher concentrations can increase the risk of irritation. However, no single concentration guarantees a product is safe for everyone. If you develop a true allergy, even a small amount can trigger a reaction.”.

It has been revealed that deciphering how much allergen is in a perfume—even in a natural or organic scent or essential oil, which isn’t necessarily a safe option for sensitive skin—is difficult. “Don’t judge a fragrance by how strong it smells,” Dr. Queller suggests. “Subtle fragrances can contain allergens, which is why the ingredient list matters more than the intensity of the scent.” If your skin is sensitive or dry, or you are rosacea- or eczema-prone, a fragrance intolerance or allergy, which often manifests as redness, itching, dryness, burning, and even swelling, hives, or blisters, is likely to form more easily, especially since she claims the skin barrier may already be impaired.

So, what’s the best way to wear a fragrance while also safeguarding your skin’s health, especially if one of the trendier skincare-infused fragrances may not be a good fit? Dr. Queller suggests applying the scent to clothing rather than directly to the skin, although she says it’s not a guarantee because fragrance can transfer to the skin. Of course, each scents’ chemical composition can vary so naturally, a bit of trial and error may be involved to determine which irritate you specifically.

The latest fragrance technology is innovative because it not only helps you avoid irritant reactions, it promises to care for a nurture skin directly. In fact, it seems we’re moving toward a world in which dual-purpose fragrances can leave you smelling good and feeling soft. It makes sense when you learn that keratinocytes—the primary cells in your epidermis—contain olfactory receptors that respond to certain fragrances, says Dr. Queller. “Skin has its own sensory biology,” she says, “and research suggests scent may influence important cellular functions, including skin regeneration and wound healing.” In fact, one study indicated that Sandalore, a sandalwood note, activates a receptor that speeds up cell growth and migration to help close cuts and sores. Another research paper found that the same pathway prolonged the growth phase of cultured human hair follicles.

It’s a welcome development. We all live extremely busy, over-scheduled lives and most of us want beauty products that do more than one thing. The upcoming Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume captures this ethos brilliantly. It combines plant-derived exosomes, thought to boost collagen, reduce inflammation, and support healthier-looking skin, with one of two scents: a warm blend of vanilla, amber, and almond or an oceanic mix of sheer musk, sea air notes, and driftwood. Similarly, Bella Hadid’s alcohol-free, essential oil-powered Orebella collection promises to hydrate skin with a bi-phase formula that simultaneously moisturizes while delivering a long-lasting scent. Another offering worth noting is Salt + Stone’s Body Mist. In six intoxicating scents, each light-as-air-mist is infused with glycerin and red algae for smooth, touchable skin. The idea of all of these is that rather than leaving your outer layer dehydrated and more susceptible to aging—a common complaint with scents formulated with alcohol—these products support dry skin and enhance its moisture levels.

Industry observers note that future Society’s unscented Base Scent follows a similar path in a different way. It works with the skin’s natural microbiome to help the body smell better. It relies on aspergillus ferment, zinc, and arginine, and you can wear it on its own or layer it over perfume to create a more neutral body scent over time. The microbiome also factors significantly into Argentum’s Les Perfumes Infinis collection. Water-based and free of potentially drying alcohol, each of the twelve scents is formulated in such a way as to not disrupt the delicate balance of bacteria naturally found on your outer layer.

Nakery Beauty Skin + Hair Exosome Perfume.

This fragrance, proven to last up to twelve hours, harnesses the power of plant-derived exosomes and an advanced hydration complex to hydrate skin and strengthen its barrier.

All of Orebella’s scents, including this brand-latest blend of creamy milk, woody amber, and fresh bergamot features a base of hydrating snow mushroom and the brand’s signature five-oil blend.

Salt & Stone Bergamot & Hinoki Body and Hair Fragrance Mist.

Salt + Stone’s body products have rightfully gained a cult following and their hair & body mists are no different. What does make them different is that they contain humectant glycerin to help skin hang onto moisture and red algae to promote smoothness. This bergamot and hinoki blend is one of their latest.

A scent with no scent? Yup. This one is formulated with prebiotics that work with your skin’s natural microbiome to keep your natural scent more consistent and balanced.

ARgENTUM Les Parfums Infinis LOVER Eau de Parfum.

Each of these alcohol- and solvent-free fragrances is gentle on skin and blended based upon one of the main elements (Earth, Air, Water). Lover, for example, is a mix of geranium, rose, and berries meant to evoke a garden after a rainfall.

According to recent reports, so, can a few spritzes of a skin-boosting fragrance achieve the same goals as a watery serum or thicker moisturizer? Potentially, but as Dr. Queller shares, it really comes down to the formulation. “A fragrance that incorporates ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, ceramides, or nourishing emollients can help improve skin hydration and support the skin barrier.” Her advice? Look beyond the label and marketing claims. “A beautifully formulated fragrance can offer skincare benefits, but that doesn’t automatically make it suitable for sensitive skin.”.

According to recent reports, what is undoubtedly true is that the skin-scent connection remains strong, perhaps stronger than ever, and this new fragrance category may provide more options for those who may not have been able to wear scent before. These next-generation fragrances go one step further than functional fragrances, which can boost your mood, productivity, and wellness, to focus on skin health in a way that was never tackled before. So go ahead and douse yourself in one of these new skin health-boosting fragrances and wait for everyone to ask, “What perfume are you wearing?”.

Taking Fish Oil to Boost Brain Health? A 2-Year Study Questions the Benefits

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine.
  • Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.
  • Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A clinical trial found that taking high dose omega-3 supplements for 2 years did not help memory or thinking skills in older adults at increased risk of Alzheimer’s.Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC led the study, which was published in eBioMedicine. Participants took either a daily high dose supplement of omega-3 fatty acid docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) or a placebo.Fish oil is one of the most familiar ways people get omega-3s. However, the supplement in this clinical trial wasn’t made from fish, Hussein Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health with Keck Medicine of USC and the study’s lead researcher, told Healthline. This article uses the broader term omega-3 supplements.The researchers found that taking supplements raised omega-3 levels in participants’ brains, yet it didn’t change their memory, thinking skills, or brain structure.Dung Trinh, MD, an internist at MemorialCare Medical Group and chief medical officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, California, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings challenge the common belief that omega-3 supplements, such as fish oil, can help prevent Alzheimer’s disease or improve memory.Millions of older adults take omega-3 supplements. In a 2017–2018 federal survey, 21.8% of U.S. adults age 60 and older reported taking an omega-3 fatty acid supplement in the past 30 days, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Getting omega-3s from food or supplements is crucial since the body cannot make them.

Keck Medicine researchers enrolled 365 adults who did not have dementia, and whose ages ranged from 55 to 80, with an average age of 66.

Subjects obtained little DHA from their diets and had at least one risk factor for dementia. Of the 365 people who enrolled, 225 completed the trial, according to the study. Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4.Participants took either 2,000 milligrams (mg) of DHA or a placebo every day. Neither participants nor researchers knew who received the supplement.

The supplement in the trial contained more than 90% DHA and about 1% EPA, Yassine noted.

Researchers found that high dose omega-3 supplements raised DHA levels in the fluid around the brain and spinal cord by 17%.

Industry observers note that both groups in the trial scored about the same on memory and thinking tests. Brain structure appeared the same in both groups.

The supplement also raised omega-3 levels in the blood. Over two years, participants’ omega-3 index, a measure of EPA and DHA in red blood cells, rose from 4.9% to 11%.“That’s a massive increase, but that doesn’t translate into clinical outcomes,” Yassine stated.DHA reached the brain equally well in people with and without the gene variant APOE4, which is linked to a higher risk of Alzheimer’s disease, according to the study.Earlier trials couldn’t tell whether DHA failed to reach the brain or reached it without helping, the study’s authors say. This trial answers that open question, since the DHA got there.“This tells us that just because a supplement reaches the brain doesn’t necessarily mean it will improve brain function or prevent cognitive decline,” Trinh said.

The lack of measurable change in memory and thinking may come down to how the body uses omega-3s, according to Yassine.He said it’s “really notable to distinguish between omega-3 metabolism and omega-3 supplements.”A supplement can raise omega-3 levels, yet the body may still break them down before they reach the right places. Obesity, smoking, and a lack of exercise can all reduce how much omega-3 gets into the brain, he said.

Some fish and fish oil supplements may offer more than omega-3s. These sources may also include other nutrients such as lutein, vitamin E, and selenium, Yassine stated.A supplement can raise the level, but if you don’t change the holistic program, just going and increasing the level by itself may not be sufficient,” he said.Researchers tend to fall into two camps on how to read the results, according to Yassine.

Some see the findings as evidence that supplements don’t work in isolation. Others argue the trial would need a longer follow-up or sicker participants to answer the question.Trinh pointed to the study’s length. “It’s also key to recognize that Alzheimer’s disease develops over decades, so a two-year study may not be long enough to determine whether DHA supplementation has any long-term preventive benefits,” he noted.

Fish oil supplements contain two omega-3 fatty acids, eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and DHA, according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (NCCIH).

Foods such as fish and flaxseed also contain omega-3s, according to the National Institutes of Health’s Office of Dietary Supplements (ODS).Research suggests omega-3s may help reduce inflammation, support heart health, and promote childhood growth and development.

Some observational studies link diets high in omega-3s with a lower risk of cognitive decline and dementia.

Recent findings suggest that researchers say omega-3s may help preserve cognition by supporting brain cells in continuing to function and maintain their membranes, according to the ODS.“Omega-3s are crucial for the brain, and we and many others have shown that having higher levels of omega-3s is associated with less Alzheimer’s pathology, better cognition, and many other protective outcomes,” Yassine said, in contrast to the trial findings.Trinh agreed. “DHA plays an essential role in maintaining healthy brain cells, and there is evidence that eating fish as part of a healthy dietary pattern may support long-term brain health,” he said.Research on omega-3s and brain health is ongoing, and there is insufficient evidence to draw firm conclusions about their effectiveness.

Some people may still benefit from a supplement, according to Yassine, including:.

Some neurologists test omega-3 levels, though the test isn’t standard, Yassine remarked.People with nutritional deficiencies or certain genetic or metabolic traits may respond differently to omega-3 supplements, and researchers still need to learn who might benefit, Trinh said.

People who already take fish oil or other omega-3 supplements for other reasons, such as high triglycerides, should make those decisions with their healthcare professionals, he remarked.

Trinh mentioned he tells his patients that “what is good for the heart is generally good for the brain.” He recommended the following healthy habits:.

“Overall, this study reminds us that there is no magic pill for preventing Alzheimer’s disease and that maintaining brain health requires a much broader approach,” Trinh remarked.

BMW just unearthed something exceedingly cool from its cellars, something that we never even knew existed: a BMW M7 Prototype.

According to recent reports, revealed via a post on BMW Classic’s Instagram and brought to broader attention to BMWBlog, the video gives us our first look ever at this performance sedan that never was. Conceived in the late 1990s, this 7-Series started life out as a 1997 BMW 740i; BMW then swapped in the 4.9-liter naturally aspirated V-8 from the E39 M5, imbuing it with 400 horsepower.

Not only does it have the M5’s engine, but BMW also paired the motor with a six-speed manual transmission. BMW notes the M7 Prototype has a top speed of 155 mph and weighs 4134 pounds. Unfortunately, that’s when the details begin to fall off, and we’re left to observe—or guess—any other info.

In a recent development, being an M7 Prototype, we suspect BMW went all-out in its M endeavors. That would mean a far sportier chassis alongside larger wheels and tires. This prototype is fitted with BBS wheels, giving it a notably more aggressive stance and look than your typical 740i. The car’s design itself remains understated, making sure to maintain its 7-Series elegance; that remarked, the rear bumper is modified to make room for the quad exhaust tips you’d see poking out the rear of the E39 M5. No 7-Series from this era featured such an outwardly aggressive exhaust exit, making it one of the few standout exterior changes to this car.

BMW also upholstered the interior with a classy tan and black two-tone. The six-speed shifter is integrated cleanly with the center console. It has a three-spoke M steering wheel, and the cluster is an M unit borrowed from the E39 M5 as well. Suffice it to say, we’re a little sad the company never brought this to production.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rinnai has released a new lineup of electric heat pump water heaters that adds wifi controls and more installation options to an appliance that can cut the energy needed for hot showers.

According to recent reports, the REHPW series comes in 50-, 65-, and 80-gallon sizes. It builds on Rinnai’s existing REHP lineup, with changes designed to make the units easier to install, monitor, and maintain.

Recent findings suggest that heat pump water heaters pull heat from the surrounding air and transfer it into the tank. Moving that heat requires less electricity than producing it with conventional electric resistance elements. There’s no fuel combustion at the appliance, although emissions from its electricity supply depend on the grid.

It has been revealed that rinnai lists a Uniform Energy Factor, or UEF, of 3.75 for the 50-gallon model and 4.0 for the two larger versions. Higher numbers mean greater efficiency under standardized testing; actual bills depend on electricity rates, hot water use, and installation conditions.

The lineup delivers up to 91 gallons of hot water in the first hour, depending on tank size. That rating includes both stored hot water and what the unit can heat during that hour – useful context when several people take consecutive showers.

There are five operating modes, 4.5 kW backup heating elements, and a variable-speed fan designed to keep noise down. The heat pump can operate with ambient air as low as 37°F.

Installation is where some of the more practical upgrades show up.

The new Rinnai heat pump water heater units have water connections on both the top and side, giving installers more options for connecting existing plumbing. Both the air intake and exhaust are on top, allowing zero side clearance where Rinnai’s installation requirements permit.

An optional ducting kit adds flexibility for tighter spaces. Carrying handles help with moving the tank into place, and the air filter slides out horizontally from the side for cleaning.

Rinnai has also added a third tank temperature sensor to the 50- and 80-gallon models to help manage hot water delivery.

Wifi adds remote monitoring and control. Rinnai’s updated Central app supports the REHPW series, including scheduling and tools to use time-of-use electricity rates to manage energy use.

According to recent reports, the units also carry CTA-2045 AC Level 2 certification for demand response. That gives compatible utility programs a way to communicate with the water heater and adjust its electricity use. Rinnai says the certification can help qualify homeowners for local and state utility demand-response rebates; availability depends on the program.

In a recent development, the series is Energy Star certified, meets NEEA Tier 4 requirements, and complies with California’s Title 24 requirements, including JA13, according to Rinnai. Warranty coverage includes 10 years for the tank and other parts, plus one year for labor.

I’m very happy with my hybrid heat pump water heater. I run it in heat pump only mode in summer and it helps cool the house for free. For anyone on the fence, especially your utility offers a rebate, it’s definitely worth looking at.

According to recent reports, rinnai directs buyers to an installer for pricing, so the upfront cost – and how much a local rebate might offset it – will require a quote. However, the REHP series price on Amazon hovers around the $2,000 mark.

Breaking: The Spectrum of Family Estrangement

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (690 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Psychologytoday

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.
  • For better or worse, I know this topic from both sides of the couch.
  • A 2025 YouGov survey found that 38 percent of American adults reported being estranged from at least one immediate family member (Orth, 2025).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Posted November 20, 2026 | Reviewed by Davia Sills.

They say to write what you know. For better or worse, I know this topic from both sides of the couch.

A 2025 YouGov survey found that 38 percent of American adults reported being estranged from at least one immediate family member (Orth, 2025). When you hear the word estrangement, you may think of Hollywood-style relational pyrotechnics, with family members storming out of the house, never to speak to one another again.

In a recent development, to be fair, that does happen. But estrangement isn’t always about screaming fights and punishing silence. Researcher Kristina Scharp (2019) describes family estrangement as a continuum involving multiple dimensions, including emotional closeness, communication, physical distance, and the desire for reconciliation.

Here are four ways family estrangement can show up.

Proximity is a factor that can contribute to closeness, but is insufficient by itself. You can live near your family, see them every week, or even reside under the same roof, but physical proximity doesn’t guarantee emotional intimacy. More simply put, seeing your family regularly doesn’t mean that you share emotional closeness with them.

With structured contact, the relationship remains intact, but you have a non-negotiable list of rules that need to be in place in order to avoid conflict either interpersonally or intrapsychically. You still maintain contact, but you’ve established limits around when, where, and how interactions happen. Structured contact may look like time limits when attending family gatherings, staying in a hotel instead of with your family, or limiting conversations to topics that don’t escalate. Structured contact can provide a way to maintain a connection while reducing exposure to harmful dynamics.

Sources indicate that with low contact, you may have rules about how and when to engage, or you may find yourself stuck in the same conversational loops on repeat. With low contact, you limit your exposure to family to only the minimum amount necessary to “check the box” of spending time with family. Low contact can often be a healthy way to preserve what remains available in a family, or it can be a way to mitigate the guilt and shame that come when you go full no contact.

Industry observers note that no contact is exactly what it sounds like. There are no phone calls, emails, texts, or visits. No contact with family can run counter to deeply held beliefs about family connection, and many people agonize for years or even decades before they do it. Contrary to public opinion, going no-contact with family is not simply a trend, and ethical psychotherapy involves carefully exploring the reasons for considering estrangement rather than encouraging it without thoughtful consideration.

Recent findings suggest that research by Reczek et al. (2023) found that periods of parent-child estrangement can be followed by renewed connection. When all parties involved are committed to the change process, even long-standing periods of estrangement may find their way toward repair. Often, when repair fails to be an option, it’s because one or more parties may be unwilling or unable to participate in the process.

Recent findings suggest that the decision to estrange yourself from family, regardless of which level of estrangement is appropriate, is one that is best made with informed supporters. Sometimes, estrangement isn’t even a choice, but the consequence of another family member’s rejection or withdrawal. While it can be a grief-laden experience, and one that should never be taken lightly, estrangement can also open up possibilities for loving and reciprocal relationships that do not cost you your energy or well-being.

In a recent development, orth, T. (2025, August 7). Family estrangement: How often and why it happens. YouGov. https://yougov.com/en-us/articles/52733-family-estrangement-how-often-and-why-it-happens.

Sources indicate that reczek, R., Stacey, L., & Thomeer, M. B. (2023). Parent–adult child estrangement in the United States by gender, race/ethnicity, and sexuality. Journal of Marriage and Family, 85(2), 494–517. https://doi.org/10.1111/jomf.12898.

According to recent reports, scharp, K. M. (2019). “You’re not welcome here”: A grounded theory of family distancing. Communication Research, 46(4), 427–455. https://doi.org/10.1177/0093650217715542.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A silicone frog built by engineers at Denmark’s Aarhus University can’t swim nearly as fast as its amphibian inspiration, but it still manages to get the job done without any moving parts. The odd invention owes its slow-but-steady aquatic maneuvering to a set of six artificial muscles specially designed to contract when exposed to near-infrared light.

Industry observers note that the team’s novel system is detailed in a study recently published in the journal Advanced Materials Technologies. Although similar setups may one day boost the capabilities of soft robots tasked with search and rescue or environmental monitoring, its creators are a bit more realistic about this frog-bot’s near-term uses.

“I could easily imagine these robots being used as toys before we see them on rescue missions,” Cecilie Ryberg, Aarhus University chemist and study co-author, stated in a profile. “I think people would have fun playing with a frog like this using a suitable light source.”.

Each of the robot’s muscles is built using crystal elastomers. These materials are specifically manufactured to contract while they are heating, and then revert back to their original shape once cooled. In this case, Ryberg and her collaborators also added a molecule that converts near-infrared light into heat. This allows the muscles to tighten after directly exposing them to a lamp. That mentioned, the process isn’t as simple as sticking the elastomers onto their model frog and dropping it into water.

According to recent reports, “Getting the six muscles to work together was a major challenge,” explained Brigitte Städler, a study co-author and Aarhus University chemist. “If they don’t contract in a coordinated way, the frog won’t swim forwards. It may simply spin around.”.

A lot of trial-and-error also went into concocting the elastomers themselves. In addition to contracting properly, the material needed the proper consistency to use in a 3D printer. To do this, Ryberg experimented with various molecular ingredients and molecule chain lengths to perfect the robot muscle recipe.

Recent findings suggest that “In a conventional 3D printer, you typically melt a solid plastic filament. Our material is more like very thick syrup or icing that you squeeze through a piping bag when decorating a cake,” said Ryberg.

The final result is a light-powered soft robot that’s quite unique, but also not in any hurry. At its best pace, the frog swam a little over three inches in about two minutes. That may not get it to its destination quickly, but the proof-of-concept successfully offers a upcoming way to think about robotic design, and the ways engineers can power their creations. Until then, there is always the potential for robo-frog toys.

Tesla is now inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use at $29,990, but the car won’t move unless you also pay $299 a month for an “Autonomy Subscription.”.

And it only works inside Tesla’s Robotaxi service areas in Texas and Florida, the same geofences that have turned out to be significantly smaller than what Tesla advertises.

Tesla’s official Robotaxi account announced the invites on X on Friday with screenshots of the order page and the invitation email.

The order page lists the Cybercab at $29,990 before taxes, with an estimated delivery of December 2026 in Austin, Texas. You need to put down a $1,000 non-refundable deposit to order.

The subscription isn’t optional. It’s pre-checked on the order page at $299 per month, with one month included, and the fine print notes “Subscription and regular vehicle maintenance required to operate.”.

According to recent reports, the email is even more direct. Its asterisk reads: “Only available in supported service areas. Subscription required for operation.”.

In a recent development, the rest is what we already knew. Two seats, a 21-inch center touchscreen, 20.1 cubic feet of cargo space, and no steering wheel or pedals. Tesla calls it “fully autonomous” and says you’ll “manage your ride in the app.”.

In a recent development, musk had promised a Cybercab “below $30,000” when he unveiled it in 2024. He technically hit it. He just didn’t mention the $3,588 a year it takes to use it. Over five years, that’s about $47,600 for a two-seater, before insurance, maintenance, taxes, and charging.

It has been revealed that tesla runs its Robotaxi service in eight cities: Austin, Dallas, Houston, Fort Worth, and San Antonio in Texas, and Miami, Orlando, and Tampa in Florida. That’s where a Cybercab can operate. Everywhere else, it’s a $30,000 sculpture in your driveway.

According to recent reports, and those service areas aren’t what Tesla says they are. Independent tracker Koby Pierce tested thousands of addresses in the Robotaxi app and found that the areas where Tesla actually accepts pickups and drop-offs are only 59% to 78% of the advertised geofences in the six cities he checked. In Austin, the very city where Tesla is delivering these cars, it’s about 59%.

In a recent development, railroad crossings are a big reason why. In Houston, the creator of Robotaxi Tracker found the app quoting about 40 minutes to go two blocks downtown because the vehicle appeared to route around rail crossings. Tesla also lists San Antonio’s airport inside its polygon but doesn’t serve it.

Then there’s the regulatory cloud. NHTSA has ordered Tesla to prove under oath that a car with no brake pedal meets federal safety standards that require one. Tesla answered on October 30 and asked that the entire response be kept confidential. NHTSA hasn’t ruled. Tesla is now selling the car to consumers anyway.

I think this is going to be a total mess. It looks like Tesla is only doing this by invitation and delivering it in Austin to prove they can deliver an “unsupervised” vehicle in 2026.

Tesla is going to sell these to fans who are excited about owning a self-driving car, and many of them will find out the limitations aren’t worth $299 a month on top of a $30,000 car.

Sure, if your monthly Uber bill is well over $300 and you live and work deep inside the geofence, maybe the math works on paper. Until you realize you have to park it somewhere once you get to your destination. Or that it can’t take you to a friend’s place two neighborhoods over. Or that a 15-minute drive turns into an hour because the car won’t cross a train track. With an Uber or a Waymo, that’s someone else’s problem. With a Cybercab, you’re paying for the privilege.

No point trying to calculate what it will cost over X years. Tesla can change that monthly fee at will anyway (and shall be expected to, considering their overall pricing history).

Industry observers note that and here’s the part that makes no sense to me. The Cybercab runs on the same AI4 computer as the current Model Y. Tesla already runs unsupervised Model Y Robotaxis in these same geofences. So why can’t the Model Y owners who already paid for “Full Self-Driving” get unsupervised operation in those same zones? Wouldn’t be even easier to turn that on these vehicles which have accumulated much more data? Tesla keeps pushing that to “next year,” right now around Q2 2027, while asking people to buy a new two-seater that can do nothing else.

If the tech works unsupervised in Austin, turn it on for the Model Y owners in Austin. If it doesn’t, why should anyone pay $47,000 over five years for a car that only works where Tesla says it does?

Like with every other Tesla product lately, the delivered version is going to be a lot more disappointing than the one that was sold on stage.

Sources indicate that your typical 2023 BMW M2 has an electronically limited top speed of 155 miles per hour. However, the optional M Driver's Package raises that limit to 177 mph. According to the Arizona Department of Public Safety (AZDPS) Highway Patrol, one M2 driver was apparently determined to explore the upper limits of his car's performance before trading it in; a state trooper clocked him traveling 170 mph on the highway, and criminal charges followed.

The incident happened on November 9, 2026, on Arizona State Route 202 near Sky Harbor Boulevard in Tempe, Arizona. According to authorities, an AZDPS Highway Patrol State Trooper spotted the BMW traveling at a high rate of speed and passing other vehicles. Using a LIDAR device, the trooper reportedly recorded the vehicle traveling 170 mph in a posted 65-mph zone—an astonishing 105 mph over the limit.

Sources indicate that police were not going to engage in a pursuit at that speed, however, and noted they decided to use the Highway Patrol Traffic Operations Center to track the vehicle's whereabouts. Eventually the BMW exited the highway, and police were then able to stop the car. At this time, the police reportedly noticed that the BMW didn’t have a license plate.

Recent findings suggest that police say the officer asked the driver how fast he thought he was going, and the man estimated his speed at approximately 110 to 115 mph. That's still far above the posted speed limit, but nowhere near the 170 mph that had him approaching Daytona 500 qualifying territory. The driver later claimed he hadn't realized just how fast he was traveling, according to authorities.

In a recent development, why was he driving so fast? He reportedly told the trooper he was planning to trade in the BMW and wanted to take it for one last drive. Hopefully his newly introduced car will be slower than the M2, because as police pointed out in their social media post, at 170 mph, the BMW was traveling approximately 250 feet every second. A crash at that speed would be devastating.

The driver was, unsurprisingly, arrested for reckless driving and endangerment, due to his excessive speed and unsafe driving behavior.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sir Patrick Stewart, best-known for portraying Captain Jean-Luc Picard in “Star Trek” and Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” film franchise, has died. He was 86.

The legendary actor and thespian passed away on October 28 after a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” according to his longtime spokesperson, Kelly Bush Novak, in a statement to The Hollywood Reporter.

He died peacefully at his home in Los Angeles, where he was receiving care from his wife, Sunny Ozell.

According to recent reports, “He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all,” Bush Novak wrote in the statement. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”.

Stewart’s acting career spanned more than six decades across theater, television, and film.

A longtime member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, he rose to international fame in 1987 with “Star Trek: The Next Generation” and later became known for his portrayal of Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 film “X-Men” and its numerous sequels.

He was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in 2010 for his contributions to drama.

Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia are two progressive neurological conditions that can affect memory, thinking, behavior, and a person’s ability to perform everyday activities.

According to the National Institute on Aging (NIA), both conditions can cause dementia, a term used to describe a decline in cognitive abilities severe enough to interfere with daily life.

Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. The condition is associated with abnormal buildups of proteins called amyloid and tau in the brain, which disrupt communication between nerve cells and contribute to their damage.

The NIA states that memory problems are often among the earliest symptoms of Alzheimer’s. As the disease progresses, people may experience increasing difficulty with language, reasoning, decision making, and recognizing familiar people.

Lewy body dementia, meanwhile, is associated with abnormal deposits of a protein called alpha-synuclein in the brain. These deposits, known as Lewy bodies, affect brain chemicals involved in thinking, movement, mood, and sleep, according to the NIA.

People with Lewy body dementia may experience changes in attention and alertness, visual hallucinations, muscle stiffness, difficulty walking, and sleep disturbances.

According to the Alzheimer’s Association, the two conditions may co-occur, and their overlapping symptoms may make diagnosis more challenging.

Currently, neither condition has a cure, but treatments are available to help manage symptoms. Certain medications can also slow cognitive decline in some people with early Alzheimer’s disease.

My days are basically a rotation of steps—commutes, errands, long walks in the name of journalism—which means I’ve become extremely picky about what earns a spot on my feet. But time after time, I keep coming back to Hoka, aka the King of Cushion.

Since the brand released in 2009, Hoka has perfected the balance between support and comfort (the number one feature in a walking shoe), says podiatrist Brad Schaeffer, DPM, foot surgeon and owner of Central Park Sole in Upcoming York City.

Hoka has not only asserted itself as a top contender in the sneaker scene, but the brand has also become a style statement, too, making ortho-looking shoes look cool with their plush cushioning. The brand churns out a bunch of styles for all sorts of activities, from running shoes to hiking boots, but Hoka’s walking shoes are some of my favorites. I get that combing through all the specs can get overwhelming, so luckily, I’ve done the legwork for you by testing and walking in Hoka sneaks for the past two years. Plus, I enlisted the help of Schaeffer and other WH editors to get the scoop on the right shoes for you.

After testing nearly every Hoka model, the Clifton 11 reigns supreme for walking. I was also a fan of the previous Clifton 10, and the newest version feels very similar. It is by far the most comfortable model in the series to date, and it’s earned a spot in my shoe rotation for its supportive yet flexible cushioning that gives me a spring in my step.

The first major difference I noticed is how light the Clifton 11 feels. Even after wearing it for several hours at a time, it doesn’t feel bulky or clunky. Which makes sense: Hoka did shave nearly half an ounce off the weight compared to the 10. The toe box is slightly more narrow, too, but I actually preferred the more secure fit because it kept my foot from sliding around without feeling cramped. If you like a little more wiggle room for your toes, I would suggest opting for the wide sizing, though.

Sources indicate that despite its lighter weight, it has an ample stack of foam padding throughout the midsole. That weightless yet cushiony feel makes it ideal for my longer walks throughout NYC. The shoe has a mild heel drop (the same as the previous model at 8 mm), which helps distribute pressure evenly across the foot.

Industry observers note that I also found that the foam absorbed impact well on both pavement and the treadmill. My feet—unfortunately plagued by plantar fasciitis—never felt fatigued wearing this shoe. There's technically a rocker shape built into the sole, but it's subtle enough that I barely notice it—instead, my stride just felt smooth and natural whether I was walking or running. I’m also a fan of the durable rubber outsole that gives plenty of traction. I never feel like I’m going to slip while wearing these, even when walking down slippery subway stairs.

So far, the Clifton 11—which was debuted alongside the new Clifton Pro— does a great job of keeping my feet comfy and supported. It’s a great shoe for anyone in need of a comfortable, everyday walking sneaker that can also handle the occasional jog (unlike the Clifton Pro, which is geared more toward high-speed running).

Read more: Hoka Clifton 11 and Clifton Pro Review.

According to recent reports, technically, the Mach 7 is a running shoe—but don’t let that marketing label fool you. I’ve walked more than 150 miles in the ultra-light, ridiculously comfortable sneaker, and not once have I felt even a bit of foot fatigue or soreness.

This style doesn’t offer any special stability features for people whose feet tend to roll while walking, but I found it still does a decent job of keeping my feet in a neutral position, despite my high arches and tendency to underpronate (or land on the outer edge of my feet).

I wear the standard size and haven’t had any problems, but Accardi prefers the wide sizing, which she finds more suitable for her bunions and ability to spread her toes. If you have similar foot concerns or just like more wiggle room, we definitely recommend the wide fit.
